## docs/connectors/file-search.md

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HelpCode-ai/anythingmcp/main/docs/connectors/file-search.md

# File Search and File Share

File Search lets an AI client search inside the documents of a folder: PDF,
Excel, Word, PowerPoint, Outlook `.msg`, `.eml` and text files on an SFTP,
FTP/FTPS, WebDAV (Nextcloud, ownCloud, NAS) or S3 server, or in a folder
mounted into a self-hosted install. AnythingMCP indexes the file names and
the text of every page, keeps the index in sync, and gives the AI tools to
search, read pages, find exact codes and hand the file to the person.

File Share turns files into temporary download links: a file from a File
Search connector, or a file an AI client wrote (a CSV, a report).

- [What you need](<https://github.com/HelpCode-ai/anythingmcp/blob/main/docs/connectors/file-search.md#what-you-need>)
- [Set up a folder](<https://github.com/HelpCode-ai/anythingmcp/blob/main/docs/connectors/file-search.md#set-up-a-folder>)
- [Sources](<https://github.com/HelpCode-ai/anythingmcp/blob/main/docs/connectors/file-search.md#sources>)
- [The tools](<https://github.com/HelpCode-ai/anythingmcp/blob/main/docs/connectors/file-search.md#the-tools>)
- [Syncing](<https://github.com/HelpCode-ai/anythingmcp/blob/main/docs/connectors/file-search.md#syncing>)
- [Limits and pauses](<https://github.com/HelpCode-ai/anythingmcp/blob/main/docs/connectors/file-search.md#limits-and-pauses>)
- [File Share](<https://github.com/HelpCode-ai/anythingmcp/blob/main/docs/connectors/file-search.md#file-share>)
- [Permissions and governance](<https://github.com/HelpCode-ai/anythingmcp/blob/main/docs/connectors/file-search.md#permissions-and-governance>)
- [Security](<https://github.com/HelpCode-ai/anythingmcp/blob/main/docs/connectors/file-search.md#security>)
- [Self-hosted setup](<https://github.com/HelpCode-ai/anythingmcp/blob/main/docs/connectors/file-search.md#self-hosted-setup>)
- [Troubleshooting](<https://github.com/HelpCode-ai/anythingmcp/blob/main/docs/connectors/file-search.md#troubleshooting>)

## What you need

| | AnythingMCP Cloud | Self-hosted |
|---|---|---|
| Plan | Every plan, the free trial included, within its limits | Enterprise (on request), an existing Starter or Team licence key, or the 30-day trial. On Community the trial opens File Search only with a registered licence key: the free Community key from **Settings → License** counts. Community has no File Search after the trial. |
| Sources | SFTP, FTP/FTPS, WebDAV, S3 on the internet | The same, plus folders mounted into the install |
| Services | Run by us | `COMPOSE_PROFILES=files` starts `files-worker` and `file-extractor` (see [Self-hosted setup](<https://github.com/HelpCode-ai/anythingmcp/blob/main/docs/connectors/file-search.md#self-hosted-setup>)) |

Only workspace administrators set up File Search connectors.

## Set up a folder

**Connectors → New → File Search** opens a five-step wizard:

1. **Source.** Pick the protocol and fill in the server, account and folder.
   Shortcuts preset Nextcloud, Synology, QNAP, Fritz!Box and Hetzner Storage
   Box.
2. **Test.** AnythingMCP connects, signs in and lists the folder before
   anything is saved. The result is a checklist (address, reachability,
   encryption, server identity, login, folder) with what to fix when a step
   fails. SFTP host keys and self-signed FTPS certificates are shown as a
   fingerprint to confirm; from then on a different key or certificate is
   refused before the password is sent.
3. **Scan.** A dry run lists the whole folder without indexing it: files per
   folder, types, years. Folders that look like archives (`Alt`, `Old`,
   `Archive…`, `Backup`) are unticked. A budget bar compares the selection
   with your plan while you tick folders, file types or an age limit. When the
   selection is larger than the plan, you cannot continue until it fits or you
   upgrade.
4. **Describe.** The connector's instructions (passed on by every MCP server
   it is on) and a one-line summary that appears in every tool description,
   drafted from the scan. With an AI model configured on the server
   (`KG_LLM_ENABLED`), the wizard can draft them with AI; it states exactly
   what is sent (folder names, file names, the first 2,000 characters of up to
   20 sample files, personal data masked). Without AI the draft is built from
   the folder structure: naming patterns of the folders, recurring
   subfolders, file types, years, language, frequent terms. Edit it before
   saving.
5. **Activate.** Tool prefix, sync interval, MCP servers. The first sync
   starts at once.

The connector's **Files** panel shows the state, progress, counts against the
plan, recent syncs, files that could not be read, the folder tree, the
description and (Enterprise) folder permissions.

## Sources

| Protocol | Notes |
|---|---|
| SFTP | Password or private key. Host key pinned on first use. |
| FTPS (explicit, port 21) / FTPS (implicit, port 990) | A certificate from a public authority is accepted; a self-signed one only by its confirmed fingerprint. Passive data connections go only to the server's own address. |
| FTP (plain) | Sends the password unencrypted; must be acknowledged, and an Enterprise policy can forbid it. |
| WebDAV | Nextcloud and ownCloud (`https://host/remote.php/dav/files/USER/`, with an app password), Synology and QNAP WebDAV, any RFC 4918 server. |
| S3 | AWS S3, DigitalOcean Spaces, MinIO, Hetzner, Wasabi. Folders are key prefixes. |
| Network folder | Self-hosted only: a folder below `FILE_SOURCE_ROOTS` (an SMB/CIFS or NFS share or a NAS volume mounted on the host and bound read-only into the containers). |

The marketplace also lists ready-made entries that open the wizard with the
right settings: S3 bucket, Nextcloud, ownCloud, Synology NAS, QNAP NAS,
Fritz!Box storage and Hetzner Storage Box.

A search for a storage system or for documents in the marketplace, on the
welcome page or from a chat (`setup_find_connectors`) also brings these
entries, next to the system's own API connector: "synology" shows the
Synology DSM connector and Synology NAS (File Search), "nas", "file server",
"Netzlaufwerk" or "pdf" show the File Search entries that fit. The marketplace
and the welcome page add a short hint with a link to the wizard; in a chat the
model gets the wizard link, since File Search is never installed from a chat.
The network folder is suggested on self-hosted installs only. SharePoint,
OneDrive, Google Drive and Dropbox searches get no File Search suggestion:
those have connectors of their own.

The wizard records anonymous funnel events (`file_search_wizard_opened`,
`file_search_test_passed` / `file_search_test_failed`,
`file_search_scan_finished`, `file_search_activated`,
`file_search_locked_shown`) in the `product_events` table, on the Cloud and
self-hosted alike. They carry the protocol, the product preset, the catalog
entry, the test's error kind and the file count as a range (`101-500`), never
a host, path, user name or file name.

SMB is not reached directly from the Cloud: port 445 does not belong on the
internet. Use SFTP or WebDAV on the NAS, or a self-hosted install.

## The tools

Each File Search connector gets these tools, named with its prefix:

| Tool | What it does |
|---|---|
| `<prefix>_guide` | How to search this folder (static) |
| `<prefix>_search` | Full-text search; files with the best page, other matching pages, a snippet and the date; filters for folder, type and dates; newest first on request |
| `<prefix>_find` | Files by name (typo-tolerant) or glob |
| `<prefix>_list` | One folder: subfolders with counts, files with size and date |
| `<prefix>_read` | The text of a file, by pages (`"1-3,7"`) or in windows of characters |
| `<prefix>_grep` | Exact search with two lines of context; spreadsheet rows come with their column names |
| `<prefix>_status` | Sync state, counts, pause reason, content summary |
| `<prefix>_view_page` | One page of a PDF, or an image file (PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, TIFF, BMP), as a picture the AI can see: for drawings, stamps, signatures and title blocks that are not in the text. Parameters `path` and `page` (default 1); the answer names the page count. Rendered at most 1600 pixels on the longest side, as JPEG up to 1.5 MB |
| `<prefix>_get_file` | The file itself as a temporary internal link (24 hours), which works in every AI client; images up to 4 MB are attached too. Without File Share on the plan, files up to 4 MB are attached and the AI names the path |
| `<prefix>_share_file` | A temporary link (internal or public); **switched off at install** |

Every tool except the share tools is read-only. The tools tell the model that
file content is data and that instructions inside files are never followed.

`_view_page` reads the file live from your server through `files-worker`,
like `_get_file`, and renders it in the isolated text extractor; on Cloud and
self-hosted alike nothing is stored. Clients such as Claude.ai show the
picture but not an attached PDF. Connectors activated before this tool
existed get it automatically when the backend starts; tools you switched off
or edited stay as they are.

Text extraction: PDF and XPS page by page; Excel (including templates,
macro workbooks and `.xlsb`), ODS and CSV row by row with the header
(`Sheet "Preise" row 2: Artikel=NO-10000 · Breite=750 · Preis=412`); Word and
ODT including templates and macro documents; PowerPoint and ODP slide by
slide, including slide shows and templates; Outlook `.msg` and `.eml` with
the text of their attachments, and `.mbox` mailboxes message by message;
EPUB chapter by chapter; the visible text of SVG drawings; the text, notes
and title-block attributes of ASCII DXF drawings; Apple Pages, Numbers and
Keynote files through their PDF preview, when they were saved with one;
RTF, legacy `.doc`/`.ppt`/`.xls`, and text formats: Markdown, JSON, XML,
HTML, logs, configuration files (YAML, TOML, INI, properties), SQL, LaTeX,
subtitles, calendars and contacts (`.ics`, `.vcf`), GPS tracks (KML, GPX),
and source code in common languages. Other files, such as images, archives,
binary DXF and DWG drawings, are found by name. Scanned PDFs are read with
OCR on Enterprise when the OCR extractor image is used.

## Syncing

Syncing runs in its own service, `files-worker`, never in the process that
answers MCP calls: a slow server or a large first sync does not slow down your
AI clients, and search keeps working on the last index during a sync.

- New and changed files are found by size and modification time (ETag on
  WebDAV and S3); unchanged content is recognised by its SHA-256 and not read
  again; deleted files leave the index.
- A big first sync runs in slices of 25 files, so other workspaces get their
  turn.
- A file that cannot be read is retried on the next syncs and, after three
  failures (at once for password-protected files), stays findable by name
  until it changes.
- **Sync now** queues a sync at once (a number per day depending on the plan).

## Limits and pauses

| | Trial (Cloud) | Starter | Team | Enterprise |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| File Search connectors | 3 | 1 | 3 | by contract (self-hosted: unlimited) |
| Indexed files, all connectors together | 2,000 | 500 | 2,000 | by contract (self-hosted: unlimited) |
| Largest file (Cloud) | 50 MB | 25 MB | 50 MB | 200 MB |
| Automatic sync | daily | daily | daily | down to every 15 minutes (self-hosted: 5) |
| Manual syncs per day | 3 | 1 | 3 | unlimited |
| OCR, folder permissions, workspace policy | – | – | – | ✓ |

The Cloud trial has the Team limits, so you can try everything before you
pick a plan. Self-hosted: the self-hosted 30-day trial has the Team limits too; file size is
set by `FILES_MAX_FILE_BYTES` (default 100 MB). Self-hosted Starter and Team
are no longer sold; existing Starter and Team keys keep the limits above, and
more comes with [Enterprise](<https://anythingmcp.com/contact?plan=enterprise>).

When a sync finds more files than the plan includes, it **pauses before
downloading anything**. The index stays as it was and the AI keeps searching
it (and is told that newer files may be missing). Administrators get one
e-mail; the Files panel shows the numbers with **Upgrade**, **Edit
selection** and **Resume**. A paused folder is checked again once a day and
resumes by itself when it fits.

When no plan includes File Search any more (a trial ended), syncing stops and
the tools answer that a licence is needed. The index is kept for 30 days.

## File Share

**Settings → File Share** lists the active links (file, access, expiry,
downloads, who created them) with **Revoke**, the plan's limits, and adds the
**File Share** connector (`share_upload`, `share_list`, `share_revoke`) that
lets AI clients publish files they write.

- **Internal** links open for signed-in members of the workspace; **public**
  links for anyone with the link. Links show an interstitial page with the
  file name, size, workspace and expiry, then download through a 60-second
  signed URL with `Content-Disposition: attachment`.
- Only a hash of each link token is stored. Expired and revoked files are
  deleted by the worker.
- Limits: Starter links last at most 24 hours, with 100 MB for the files of
  all active links together and 10 MB per file; Team 7 days, 2 GB, 50 MB. The
  Cloud trial has the Team limits. On the Cloud, program files (`.exe`, `.msi`,
  `.js`, …) cannot be shared.

## Permissions and governance

- Who sees the tools follows the MCP roles, as for every connector.
- **Folder permissions (Enterprise):** allow or deny folders per role inside
  one connector.
  - A role without rules sees everything. Adding a rule for one role never
    changes what other roles see.
  - Allow rules limit a role to those folders (and their subfolders). A user
    with several roles sees the folders any of their roles allows.
  - Deny rules hide a folder and always win, also over an allow.
  - Workspace administrators see every folder.
  - Calls with an MCP API key are not tied to a user, so folder rules do not
    apply to them: give such keys only to servers whose folders everyone with
    the key may see.

  Without Enterprise, connect each folder as its own connector and give it to
  the right roles.
- **Workspace policy (Enterprise):** public links on/off, longest link
  validity, AI drafting on/off, plain FTP on/off.
- Every tool call is in the audit log as usual.

## Security

- Every query on the index is filtered by workspace and connector, and the
  `file_*` tables have Row-Level Security enforced through a dedicated
  database role, so a query that forgot its filter returns nothing of another
  workspace. On a managed database where the application user may not create
  roles, the migration skips the role and the policies apply to the
  application user itself (as long as it is not a superuser).
- Every query on the `file_*` tables, the worker's cross-workspace jobs
  included (picking due syncs and scans, lease renewal, cleanups, deleting
  expired share files), runs one workspace at a time with that workspace set
  for the transaction. No job needs a database user that bypasses
  Row-Level Security. A share link is looked up by the SHA-256 of its token
  under a read-only policy that shows only the row with that hash.
- Self-hosted with an external database: see
  [Database user](<https://github.com/HelpCode-ai/anythingmcp/blob/main/docs/connectors/file-search.md#database-user>) below.
- Credentials are stored encrypted and decrypted only in `files-worker`; the
  text extractor runs on an internal network with no route out, no database
  and no secrets, read-only, without capabilities.
- On the Cloud, hosts must be public (the SSRF policy also checks redirects
  and the resolved address).

## Self-hosted setup

1. Generate the secrets and add them to `.env`:
   ```bash
   echo "FILES_WORKER_URL=http://files-worker:8891" >> .env
   echo "FILES_WORKER_TOKEN=$(openssl rand -hex 24)" >> .env
   echo "FILE_EXTRACTOR_TOKEN=$(openssl rand -hex 24)" >> .env
   echo "COMPOSE_PROFILES=files" >> .env
   ```
2. For network folders, mount the share on the host (read-only), bind it into
   `app` and `files-worker` (see the comment in `docker-compose.yml`) and set
   `FILE_SOURCE_ROOTS=/mnt/knowledge`.
3. `docker compose up -d`. **Connectors → New → File Search** shows whether the
   worker and the extractor are reachable.

### Database user

File Search works with an ordinary database user: neither superuser nor
`BYPASSRLS` is needed. The default Docker setup connects as the database
owner (a superuser), which works too.

- **`amcp_files`** is a `NOLOGIN` role without `BYPASSRLS` that the File
  Search migration creates and grants to the migrating user. Every query on
  the `file_*` tables switches to it for its transaction (`SET LOCAL ROLE`),
  so the Row-Level Security policies apply even to a superuser. It has
  `SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE` on the `file_*` tables, the `file_chunks`
  id sequence, and `SELECT` on `connectors (id, organization_id, type,
  is_active, name)`.
- **Managed databases** (RDS, Azure, Cloud SQL, Supabase…): if the migrating
  user may not create roles, the migration skips `amcp_files` with a notice
  and the policies apply to the application user directly. That is enough as
  long as the user does not bypass RLS. Give the application user the
  ordinary rights on the schema, for example:
  ```sql
  GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA public TO app_user;
  GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public TO app_user;
  GRANT USAGE, SELECT ON ALL SEQUENCES IN SCHEMA public TO app_user;
  ```
  If an administrator creates `amcp_files` later, also grant it to the
  application user (`GRANT amcp_files TO app_user;`) and give it the rights
  listed above.
- Run the migrations with the same user the application uses, or with the
  owner of the tables, so later migrations can alter them.
- At start the `files-worker` log names the mode in use: `role amcp_files`,
  `application user subject to Row-Level Security`, or `application user
  bypassing Row-Level Security` (superuser or `BYPASSRLS` without
  `amcp_files`: then only the queries' workspace filters separate
  workspaces). It warns once when File Search folders exist but no source is
  visible, which means the user lacks rights on the `file_*` tables.

The sync engine (`packages/backend/src/ee/file-search`) and the extractor
(`deploy/ee/file-extractor`) are under the AnythingMCP Commercial License.
All environment variables are listed in `.env.example` under "File Search
and File Share".

## Troubleshooting

| Message | What to do |
|---|---|
| "File Search is not running on this server" | Start the `files` profile; check `FILES_WORKER_URL` and that both tokens are set. |
| "This address is in a private network" | The Cloud cannot reach internal hosts. Self-hosted: add the host to the outbound allowlist (Admin → Settings or `SSRF_ALLOWED_HOSTS`). |
| "The server presented a different host key/certificate" | The server was reinstalled or someone is in between. Check with the server's administrator before confirming the new fingerprint (Files panel → Edit selection → back to Test). |
| "Sync paused: the folder outgrew your plan" | Untick folders or file types (Edit selection) or upgrade. |
| A file "could not be read" | Password-protected, damaged or a scan without OCR. It stays findable by name. |

## docs/connectors/graphql.md

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HelpCode-ai/anythingmcp/main/docs/connectors/graphql.md

# GraphQL to MCP

AnythingMCP turns any GraphQL API into MCP tools for Claude, ChatGPT and Copilot without code. Introspection generates a tool per query and mutation, or you define the operations yourself, with the same auth, audit and response mapping as every other connector.

[Back to README](<https://github.com/HelpCode-ai/anythingmcp/blob/main/README.md>)

---

## Overview

The GraphQL connector exposes GraphQL queries and mutations as individual MCP tools. It supports automatic tool generation via introspection and manual query definition.

**Keywords:** GraphQL to MCP, GraphQL MCP bridge, GraphQL API to MCP server, GraphQL introspection MCP

---

## Creating a GraphQL Connector

### Via Web UI

1. Go to **Connectors** > **New Connector**
2. Select **GraphQL** as the type
3. Enter the **GraphQL Endpoint URL** (e.g., `https://api.example.com/graphql`)
4. Configure authentication if needed
5. Click **Create**

### Via API

```bash
curl -s http://localhost:4000/api/connectors \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "name": "My GraphQL API",
    "type": "GRAPHQL",
    "baseUrl": "https://api.example.com/graphql",
    "authType": "BEARER_TOKEN",
    "authConfig": {
      "token": "your-graphql-token"
    }
  }'
```

---

## Importing Tools via Introspection

Provide the GraphQL endpoint and AnythingMCP will run an introspection query to auto-generate tools for each:
- **Query field** → Read-only tool
- **Mutation field** → Write tool

```bash
curl -s http://localhost:4000/api/connectors/$CONNECTOR_ID/import \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "source": "graphql",
    "url": "https://api.example.com/graphql"
  }'
```

Each generated tool includes:
- Typed parameters from the GraphQL schema
- The full query/mutation string
- Variable mapping

---

## Tool Configuration

### Endpoint Mapping for GraphQL

GraphQL tools use a specific mapping format:

```json
{
  "method": "query",
  "path": "query GetUser($id: ID!) { user(id: $id) { id name email } }",
  "queryParams": {
    "id": "$user_id"
  }
}
```

| Field | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| `method` | `query` or `mutation` |
| `path` | The GraphQL query/mutation string |
| `queryParams` | Maps tool parameters to GraphQL variables |
| `headers` | Optional HTTP headers for the request |

### Manual Tool Definition

```json
{
  "name": "search_products",
  "description": "Search products by name and category",
  "parameters": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "query": { "type": "string", "description": "Search term" },
      "category": { "type": "string", "description": "Category filter" },
      "limit": { "type": "integer", "description": "Max results" }
    },
    "required": ["query"]
  },
  "endpointMapping": {
    "method": "query",
    "path": "query SearchProducts($query: String!, $category: String, $limit: Int) { searchProducts(query: $query, category: $category, limit: $limit) { id name price category } }",
    "queryParams": {
      "query": "$query",
      "category": "$category",
      "limit": "$limit"
    }
  }
}
```

---

## Authentication

GraphQL connectors support all standard auth types:

| Auth Type | Config |
|-----------|--------|
| **Bearer Token** | `"authType": "BEARER_TOKEN", "authConfig": {"token": "..."}` |
| **API Key** | `"authType": "API_KEY", "authConfig": {"key": "X-API-Key", "value": "..."}` |
| **Basic Auth** | `"authType": "BASIC_AUTH", "authConfig": {"username": "...", "password": "..."}` |
| **OAuth2** | `"authType": "OAUTH2", "authConfig": {"clientId": "...", "clientSecret": "...", "authorizationUrl": "...", "tokenUrl": "...", "scopes": "read write"}` |

### OAuth2 Authorization Flow

OAuth2 connectors use the **Authorization Code + PKCE** flow. After creating the connector, click **Authorize with Provider** on the detail page to start the flow. Set `http://localhost:4000/api/mcp-oauth/callback` as the redirect URI in your provider. On 401 responses, the engine automatically refreshes the token and retries.

---

## Example: GitHub GraphQL API

```bash
# 1. Create connector
CONNECTOR_ID=$(curl -s http://localhost:4000/api/connectors \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "name": "GitHub GraphQL",
    "type": "GRAPHQL",
    "baseUrl": "https://api.github.com/graphql",
    "authType": "BEARER_TOKEN",
    "authConfig": {"token": "ghp_your_github_token"}
  }' | jq -r '.id')

# 2. Create a tool manually
curl -s http://localhost:4000/api/connectors/$CONNECTOR_ID/tools \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "name": "get_repo_info",
    "description": "Get GitHub repository information",
    "parameters": {
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {
        "owner": { "type": "string", "description": "Repository owner" },
        "name": { "type": "string", "description": "Repository name" }
      },
      "required": ["owner", "name"]
    },
    "endpointMapping": {
      "method": "query",
      "path": "query GetRepo($owner: String!, $name: String!) { repository(owner: $owner, name: $name) { name description stargazerCount forkCount primaryLanguage { name } } }",
      "queryParams": {
        "owner": "$owner",
        "name": "$name"
      }
    }
  }'
```

## Troubleshooting

| Issue | Solution |
|-------|----------|
| Introspection fails | Ensure the endpoint allows introspection queries and auth is configured |
| Variables not mapped | Verify `queryParams` keys match GraphQL variable names (case-sensitive) |
| Mutation not working | Set `"method": "mutation"` in the endpoint mapping |

## docs/connectors/login-token-auth.md

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HelpCode-ai/anythingmcp/main/docs/connectors/login-token-auth.md

# LOGIN_TOKEN Authentication

> Reference for adapter authors building connectors against APIs that:
>
> - Issue a long-lived bearer token in exchange for a credentials POST
> - Optionally require the password to be bcrypt-hashed client-side with a salt fetched from the remote service (Sorare-style)
> - Want automatic token caching, proactive refresh, and re-login on 401 with no per-call boilerplate

[Back to README](<https://github.com/HelpCode-ai/anythingmcp/blob/main/README.md>) | [Tool Definition](<https://github.com/HelpCode-ai/anythingmcp/blob/main/docs/tool-definition.md>)

---

## When to use `LOGIN_TOKEN`

| Scenario | Use |
|---|---|
| Static API key in a header | `API_KEY` |
| User-provided bearer JWT, no rotation | `BEARER_TOKEN` |
| HTTP Basic | `BASIC_AUTH` |
| OAuth2 Authorization Code / Client Credentials with refresh tokens | `OAUTH2` |
| **POST `{username, password}` → receive bearer good for hours/days** | **`LOGIN_TOKEN`** |
| **Client-side bcrypt against a per-account salt before login** | **`LOGIN_TOKEN`** |

If your provider already speaks OAuth2, prefer `OAUTH2` — it has standardised refresh, scope, and PKCE handling.

---

## How the engine flows

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ first tool call                                                     │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    │
    ├─ cache hit (memory) → use cached token ──────────────────────┐
    │                                                              │
    ├─ cache miss → DB lookup ─ row present, not near expiry ──────┤
    │                                                              │
    └─ cache miss + DB miss / expired:                             │
         1. resolveSalt()      (saltSource.fetch OR static)        │
         2. preparePassword()  (bcrypt OR passthrough)             │
         3. POST loginBody     (interpolate ${...} placeholders)   │
         4. extract token + expiry                                 │
         5. cache in-memory + upsert connector_auth_cache row      │
                                                                   │
                                                          ┌────────┘
                                                          ▼
                                      inject Authorization header (+ extraHeaders)
                                                          ▼
                                      execute the tool call ─────► API
                                                          │
                                                          ▼
                                              response 401? ──► forceRelogin() + retry once
```

The token cache is keyed by `connectorId` (when available) or by `loginUrl|username`. A per-key mutex prevents concurrent refresh storms.

---

## `authConfig` field reference

```jsonc
{
  // ─── Login endpoint ────────────────────────────────────────────
  "loginUrl": "https://api.example.com/graphql",
  "loginMethod": "POST",                     // GET | POST (default POST)
  "loginHeaders": { "X-App": "anythingmcp" }, // static headers for the login call
  "loginBasicAuth": true,                    // optional: send Authorization: Basic base64(username:password)
                                             // on the login call only (Wazuh). The password is then not
                                             // offered to templates, no body is sent without loginBody, and
                                             // an Authorization in loginHeaders is refused, as are signedJwt
                                             // and bcrypt passwordHashing.

  // ─── Body: prefer structured `loginBody` (recursive ${name} substitution) ─
  "loginBody": {
    "query": "mutation Login($email: String!, $password: String!) { signIn(input: {email: $email, password: $password}) { token } }",
    "variables": {
      "email": "${username}",
      "password": "${passwordHashed}"
    }
  },
  // …or a raw string template (only for very simple JSON bodies):
  "loginBodyTemplate": "{\"u\":\"${username}\",\"p\":\"${passwordHashed}\"}",

  // ─── Credentials & client identity ─────────────────────────────
  "username": "{{SERVICE_EMAIL}}",
  "password": "{{SERVICE_PASSWORD}}",
  "aud":      "{{SERVICE_AUD}}",     // optional; exposed in ${aud} for templates/headers
  "otp":      "{{SERVICE_OTP}}",     // optional 2FA code

  // ─── Client-side password preprocessing ────────────────────────
  "passwordHashing": {
    "scheme": "bcrypt",              // bcrypt | none
    "saltSource": {                  // required when scheme=bcrypt
      "type": "fetch",               // fetch | static
      "method": "GET",
      "url": "https://api.example.com/api/v1/users/${username}",
      "headers": { },
      "responsePath": "salt",        // JSON path to salt in the response
      "value": "$2a$11$..."          // only when type=static
    },
    "outputParam": "passwordHashed"  // name exposed to the body template (default: passwordHashed)
  },

  // ─── Or: a JWT signed with the account's private key (no password) ─
  "signedJwt": {
    "privateKey": "{{SERVICE_PRIVATE_KEY}}", // PEM, PKCS#1 / PKCS#8 / SEC1
    "algorithm":  "RS256",                   // RS256 (default) | RS384 | RS512 | PS256 | ES256 | ES384
    "claims":     { "sub": "{{SERVICE_KEY_ID}}" },
    "keyId":      "…",                       // optional `kid` header
    "ttlSeconds": 300,                       // optional; adds exp = iat + ttlSeconds
    "outputParam": "signedJwt"               // name exposed to the body template (default: signedJwt)
  },

  // ─── Where to find the token & expiry in the login response ────
  "tokenJsonPath":  "data.signIn.jwtToken.token",   // or a list, see below
  "expiryJsonPath": "data.signIn.jwtToken.expiredAt",
  "audJsonPath":    "data.signIn.jwtToken.aud",      // optional — overrides authConfig.aud
  "expiryFormat":   "iso8601",                       // iso8601 | unix | ttl_seconds
  "tokenTTLSeconds": 2592000,                        // fallback when expiry is absent (30 days)

  // ─── Or: the session is a cookie the login sets ────────────────
  "tokenSource": "cookie",                           // body (default) | cookie
  "cookieName":  "B1SESSION",                        // the cookie whose value is ${token}
  "cookieMode":  "single",                           // single (default) | all — see below

  // ─── Re-login policy ───────────────────────────────────────────
  "refreshOn401": true,                              // re-login on a 401 and retry once (default true)
  "proactiveRefreshSeconds": 86400,                  // re-login when this much remains (default 24 h)

  // ─── Header injection for downstream tool calls ────────────────
  "headerName":     "Authorization",                 // default Authorization
  "headerTemplate": "Bearer ${token}",               // default "Bearer ${token}"
  "extraHeaders": {
    "JWT-AUD": "${aud}"
  }
}
```

### Several candidate token paths

When the vendor does not document the login answer, `tokenJsonPath` can be a
list of paths, tried in order; the first that holds a non-empty string is the
token. `"."` takes the whole body, for a login that answers with a bare
string. A login that finds none fails with every path named (or with the
service's own refusal message, when the body carries one). A single string
works as before.

```json
"tokenJsonPath": ["AuthenticationResult.IdToken", "IdToken", "idToken", "data.idToken", "token", "."]
```

### Placeholders available in templates

The placeholders below are substituted by the engine when rendering `loginBody` / `loginBodyTemplate` and the salt-source URL:

| Placeholder | Source |
|---|---|
| `${username}` | `authConfig.username` |
| `${password}` | `authConfig.password` (plain, **before** hashing) |
| `${passwordHashed}` | output of the password preprocessor (renamed via `outputParam`) |
| `${aud}` | `authConfig.aud` |
| `${otp}` | `authConfig.otp` |
| `${signedJwt}` | a JWT signed for this login (see below; renamed via `outputParam`) |

In `headerTemplate` and `extraHeaders`, only `${token}`, `${aud}` and `${uuid}` are available. `${token}` and `${aud}` refer to the issued token, not the credentials. `${uuid}` is a new random UUID for every API request (the same value wherever it appears in that request), for APIs that want a unique request or correlation id on each call. In `loginHeaders`, `${uuid}` is the only placeholder and gives each login its own UUID.

A `loginBody` that is a string is sent as is. Together with `"Content-Type": "application/x-www-form-urlencoded"` in `loginHeaders` that covers OAuth-style token endpoints which take a form body, such as Walmart's client-credentials call (`"loginBody": "grant_type=client_credentials"` with `loginBasicAuth: true`).

### Signed JWT logins

Some APIs take no password: the client signs a short JWT with the private key
of a service account and posts it to the login endpoint (noon's Partner API:
RS256, `sub` = the key id, then the session comes back as cookies). With
`signedJwt` set, `username` and `password` are not required, and every login
signs a new token: `iat` is the current time in whole seconds, `jti` a random
UUID, then the configured `claims`; `exp` is added only when `ttlSeconds` is
set. A claim whose `{{VARIABLE}}` has no value stops the login with an error
that names it. The key is read as for OAuth2 `private_key_jwt` client
assertions: a PEM pasted on one line or with literal `\n` works, an encrypted
key is refused, and no error message contains key material.

```json
"loginBody": { "token": "${signedJwt}", "default_project_code": "{{NOON_PROJECT_CODE}}" },
"signedJwt": { "privateKey": "{{NOON_PRIVATE_KEY}}", "algorithm": "RS256", "claims": { "sub": "{{NOON_KEY_ID}}" } },
"tokenSource": "cookie",
"cookieMode": "all"
```

### Expiry formats

| `expiryFormat` | Value at `expiryJsonPath` |
|---|---|
| `iso8601` *(default)* | `"2026-06-17T08:34:21Z"` |
| `unix` | Seconds (≤1e12) or milliseconds since epoch |
| `ttl_seconds` | Lifetime in seconds from now |

If `expiryJsonPath` is missing or unresolvable, the engine falls back to `tokenTTLSeconds` (default 30 days).

### Session cookies

With `"tokenSource": "cookie"` the token is read from the login response's
`Set-Cookie` headers instead of its body.

- `"cookieMode": "single"` (default): `${token}` is the value of the cookie
  named `cookieName`, so the header is written as
  `"headerName": "Cookie", "headerTemplate": "B1SESSION=${token}"` (SAP
  Business One Service Layer).
- `"cookieMode": "all"`: `${token}` is every cookie the login set, already
  formatted as `name=value; name2=value2`, so the header is
  `"headerName": "Cookie", "headerTemplate": "${token}"`. Use it when the
  login sets more than one cookie the API needs, typically a session cookie
  plus a load-balancer cookie that pins the session to one node (SAP
  Signavio). Attributes are dropped, a cookie set twice keeps its last value,
  and a cookie the response deletes (empty value or `Max-Age` of 0 or less)
  is left out. `cookieName` is optional here; when set, the login fails unless
  that cookie is among them.

The body can still supply `${aud}` through `audJsonPath` (`"."` takes the
whole body, for logins that answer with a bare token string).

---

## Security notes

- **Private keys never leave the server.** With `signedJwt`, only the signed token is sent; the key stays in encrypted storage like a password.
- **Plain passwords never leave the server.** Only the bcrypt hash is sent over the wire; the plain password lives only in encrypted `authConfig` storage.
- The encrypted `authConfig` is decrypted in-process at request time and never logged.
- Tokens persisted in `connector_auth_cache` are encrypted with the same AES-256-GCM key (`ENCRYPTION_KEY` env var).
- The salt-fetch and login URLs are passed through the SSRF guard (`assertSafeOutboundUrl`) before each request — they cannot point to private addresses.
- `${...}` placeholders are substituted as exact values, not eval'd; prototype-pollution keys (`__proto__`, `constructor`, `prototype`) are rejected by the raw-string renderer.

## docs/connectors/mcp-bridge.md

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HelpCode-ai/anythingmcp/main/docs/connectors/mcp-bridge.md

# MCP Bridge Connector — MCP-to-MCP Gateway

> Aggregate multiple MCP servers into one. Create a unified MCP gateway that proxies tools from other MCP servers.

[Back to README](<https://github.com/HelpCode-ai/anythingmcp/blob/main/README.md>)

---

## Overview

The MCP Bridge connector lets you connect to **other MCP servers** and re-expose their tools through AnythingMCP. This creates a unified gateway where AI clients connect to a single MCP endpoint and access tools from multiple backend MCP servers.

**Keywords:** MCP gateway, MCP proxy, MCP aggregator, MCP middleware, MCP-to-MCP bridge, MCP server federation, MCP hub

---

## Use Cases

- **MCP Aggregation** — Combine tools from multiple MCP servers into one endpoint
- **MCP Proxy** — Add authentication, rate limiting, and audit logging in front of existing MCP servers
- **MCP Gateway** — Single entry point for AI clients to access all your MCP tools
- **Tool Curation** — Select which tools from remote MCP servers to expose

---

## Creating an MCP Bridge Connector

### Via Web UI

1. Go to **Connectors** > **New Connector**
2. Select **MCP** as the type
3. Enter the **Remote MCP Server URL** — the *complete* endpoint URL, including its path (e.g., `http://other-mcp-server:3000/mcp`)
4. Configure authentication for the remote server
5. Click **Create**

### Via API

```bash
curl -s http://localhost:4000/api/connectors \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "name": "Remote MCP Server",
    "type": "MCP",
    "baseUrl": "http://other-mcp-server:3000/mcp",
    "authType": "BEARER_TOKEN",
    "authConfig": {
      "token": "remote-server-token"
    }
  }'
```

### The base URL is the endpoint

Whatever path you put in the base URL is the path AnythingMCP calls. This matters for
providers that do not serve MCP at the root of their host:

| Remote server | Base URL to enter |
|---------------|-------------------|
| Most hosted servers | `https://mcp.example.com/mcp` |
| Snowflake managed MCP server | `https://<account>.snowflakecomputing.com/api/v2/databases/<db>/schemas/<schema>/mcp-servers/<name>` |
| Another AnythingMCP instance | `https://your-anythingmcp.example.com/mcp/<serverId>` |
| Zoho MCP | `https://<workspace>.zohomcp.com/mcp/<token>/message` |

A base URL with **no** path (`https://mcp.example.com`) falls back to `/mcp`, which is where
most servers listen.

> **Changed behaviour.** Releases up to v0.4.2 always POSTed to `<origin>/mcp` and silently
> discarded the base URL's path, so servers hosted under a path could never be reached
> ([#501](<https://github.com/HelpCode-ai/anythingmcp/issues/501>)). If you had worked around
> this by leaving an unrelated path in the base URL, set it back to the bare host.

---

## How It Works

1. AnythingMCP connects to the remote MCP server
2. It discovers available tools on the remote server
3. Tools are registered in the local ToolRegistry
4. When an AI client calls a bridged tool, AnythingMCP:
   - Forwards the tool call to the remote MCP server
   - Passes parameters through, and fills in from the connector's environment variables only
     the parameters the remote tool's schema names (a variable called `owner` fills `owner`;
     the connector's own key or token is never sent as a tool argument)
   - Returns the response

### Endpoint Mapping

MCP bridge tools use a simple mapping:

```json
{
  "method": "remote_tool_name",
  "bodyMapping": {
    "param1": "$param1",
    "param2": "$param2"
  }
}
```

| Field | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| `method` | The tool name on the remote MCP server |
| `bodyMapping` | Maps local parameters to remote tool parameters |
| `path` | Optional. Overrides the endpoint for this tool only. A leading `/` is resolved against the host, a relative value is appended to the base URL's path, and a full `https://…` URL is used verbatim. The default `/mcp` means "use the connector's base URL". |

---

## Authentication

The MCP Bridge supports automatic token refresh for OAuth2-protected remote servers.

| Auth Type | Use Case |
|-----------|----------|
| **Bearer Token** | Static token for the remote MCP server (Linear, GitHub, Stripe, Firecrawl, Apify keys) |
| **Basic Auth** | `Authorization: Basic base64(username:password)`, e.g. an Atlassian personal API token as `email:token` |
| **OAuth2** | Sign in at the provider ("Authorize with Provider"); tokens refresh automatically |
| **API Key** | API key in a header of your choice |
| **None** | For unprotected local MCP servers |

### OAuth2 against a remote MCP server

"Authorize with Provider" on an MCP connector:

1. **Discovers** the server's OAuth metadata: the RFC 9728 protected-resource document
   (path-inserted, then at the root of the host), the authorization server it names (RFC 8414,
   then OpenID Connect discovery), and finally the origin-level
   `/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server` of older servers.
2. **Takes the endpoints as published.** An authorization server on another host is legitimate
   (Stripe's is `access.stripe.com`, Apify's `console.apify.com`). Only an endpoint on a host
   that cannot be reached from outside (loopback, private address, `.local`, a single-label
   Docker name) is moved onto the MCP server's own origin: that is what a self-hosted server with
   a wrong `OAUTH_SERVER_URL` advertises. Token and registration requests go through the SSRF
   guard; the authorization endpoint must be `http(s)`.
3. **Picks the client**: a pre-registered one (see `mcpOAuth` below), else one obtained by
   dynamic client registration (RFC 7591), else the client ID/secret stored in the connector's
   OAuth settings. A registered client is kept in the connector's encrypted auth config and
   reused on the next authorization; it is registered again only when the server, the callback
   URL or the secret's expiry changes, or the provider refuses it (`invalid_client`).
   Registration asks for the token endpoint auth method the server supports: `none` (a public
   client, no secret) where that is all it offers.
4. **Sends** PKCE S256, the `scope` (the protected resource's `scopes_supported`, else the
   authorization server's) and the RFC 8707 `resource` indicator on the authorization request,
   the code exchange and every refresh, whenever the server publishes a protected-resource
   document.
5. **Imports the tools** the server lists once the token is stored. A connector installed from
   a catalog adapter goes through the same policy as the install: tools the catalog switches off
   arrive switched off, catalog annotations fill what the server leaves out, the tool prefix
   applies.

The redirect URI to register with a provider is `<SERVER_URL>/api/mcp-oauth/callback`
(`GET /api/connectors/oauth/redirect-uri` returns it).

With **AnythingMCP Enterprise**, an OAuth2 connector can require every user to
sign in with their own account instead of sharing one authorization, so the
remote server answers each user with their own permissions. See
[Per-user sign-in](<https://github.com/HelpCode-ai/anythingmcp/blob/main/docs/connectors/per-user-sign-in.md>).

### Connector settings (`connector.config`)

A catalog adapter sets these under `connector.config`; they are copied into the connector at
install. Through the API they can be set on any MCP connector.

| Key | Meaning |
|-----|---------|
| `mcpPath` | Endpoint path when the base URL cannot say it. A base URL without a path means `<origin>/mcp`, so a server at the root of its host (Stripe, Apify) sets `"/"`. |
| `mcpToolPrefix` | Prepended to the remote tool names (`linear_` turns `list_issues` into `linear_list_issues`), so two bridges with tools of the same name can share an MCP server. Characters outside `[A-Za-z0-9_]` become `_`, and a name that already starts with the prefix keeps it once. Calls still use the remote name. |
| `mcpOAuth` | How "Authorize with Provider" works for this connector, below. |

`mcpOAuth` (every field optional):

```json
"mcpOAuth": {
  "registration": "auto",
  "clientId": "{{ACME_CLIENT_ID}}",
  "clientSecret": "{{ACME_CLIENT_SECRET}}",
  "scope": "mcp_api refresh_token",
  "tokenAuthMethod": "client_secret_post",
  "resource": true
}
```

| Field | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `registration` | `auto` (default): the pre-registered client when `clientId` resolves to a value, else dynamic registration, else the client stored in the OAuth settings. `dcr`: always dynamic registration. `preregistered`: never dynamic registration, even if the server advertises it (Salesforce does, and refuses it for MCP). |
| `clientId`, `clientSecret` | A client the user registered with the provider, normally `{{VAR}}` placeholders. They are resolved from the connector's environment variables when the user clicks Authorize, so values typed after install are used. With empty variables the error names them and the redirect URI to register. |
| `scope` | The scope to request. `""` sends no scope at all (Asana asks for that). Absent: the protected resource's scopes, else the authorization server's. A scope typed in the connector's OAuth settings wins. |
| `tokenAuthMethod` | `none`, `client_secret_post` or `client_secret_basic`: for a pre-registered client, how it authenticates at the token endpoint; for dynamic registration, the method to register with. |
| `resource` | RFC 8707 indicator. Default: sent when the server publishes a protected-resource document, with that document's `resource` (else the MCP URL). `true` always sends it, `false` never, a string sends that value. |

### Vendor MCP servers in the catalog

These catalog adapters bridge a vendor's official remote MCP server. At install AnythingMCP lists
the tools of the server (the catalog keeps a snapshot for the store and as the fallback when the
server cannot be reached). Click **Discover tools** on the connector after the vendor adds tools.
The setup check runs the adapter's `probe` tool, or lists the server's tools when the adapter
declares none, so a refused token is reported on the setup form before anything is saved.

| Adapter | Endpoint | Auth |
|---------|----------|------|
| Splunk | `https://<host>:8089/services/mcp` | Bearer (encrypted MCP token) |
| Linear | `https://mcp.linear.app/mcp` | Bearer (API key) |
| GitHub | `https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/` | Bearer (personal access token) |
| Stripe | `https://mcp.stripe.com` (root, `mcpPath: "/"`) | Bearer (agent restricted key) |
| Atlassian (Jira, Confluence) | `https://mcp.atlassian.com/v2/mcp` | Basic (email + API token), or Bearer for a service account key |
| Snowflake | `https://<account>/api/v2/databases/<db>/schemas/<schema>/mcp-servers/<name>` | Bearer (programmatic access token) |
| Firecrawl | `https://mcp.firecrawl.dev/v2/mcp` | Bearer (API key) |
| Apify | `https://mcp.apify.com` (root, `mcpPath: "/"`) | Bearer (API token) |
| Notion | `https://mcp.notion.com/mcp` | OAuth2, dynamic registration |
| Helium 10 | `https://mcp.helium10.com/mcp` | OAuth2, dynamic registration |

One authorization serves every caller of a connector: whoever clicks "Authorize" is the identity
the tools act as. For per-user tools (Notion, Slack, Salesforce) use a dedicated account until
per-user tokens exist.

---

## Architecture Example

```
  Claude Desktop ─┐
  ChatGPT ────────┤
  Cursor ─────────┤
                  ▼
           AnythingMCP (Gateway)
           ┌───────────────────┐
           │ MCP Bridge #1 ────│──► File System MCP Server
           │ MCP Bridge #2 ────│──► Slack MCP Server
           │ MCP Bridge #3 ────│──► Custom MCP Server
           │ REST Connector ───│──► Your REST API
           │ DB Connector ─────│──► PostgreSQL / MySQL / MongoDB / ...
           └───────────────────┘
```

All AI clients connect to **one** AnythingMCP endpoint and get access to tools from all connected servers.

---

## Benefits Over Direct Connection

| Feature | Direct MCP | Via AnythingMCP |
|---------|-----------|-----------------|
| Auth & rate limiting | Per-server config | Centralized |
| Audit logging | None | Every invocation logged |
| Role-based access | None | Tool-level whitelisting |
| API key management | None | Per-user keys |
| Response caching | None | Redis caching |
| Tool curation | All or nothing | Select which tools to expose |

## docs/connectors/odata.md

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HelpCode-ai/anythingmcp/main/docs/connectors/odata.md

# OData to MCP

AnythingMCP connects Claude, ChatGPT and Copilot to OData V2 and V4 services through MCP, with SAP Gateway (S/4HANA, ECC, BW) as a first-class case. An OData connector reads each service's `$metadata`, so the model sees entity sets, keys and fields with their business labels, the currency or unit that belongs to each amount, and which fields are dimensions or measures, before it asks for a single row.

[Back to README](<https://github.com/HelpCode-ai/anythingmcp/blob/main/README.md>) · [REST connector](<https://github.com/HelpCode-ai/anythingmcp/blob/main/docs/connectors/rest.md>) · [SAP HANA](<https://github.com/HelpCode-ai/anythingmcp/blob/main/docs/connectors/sap-hana.md>)

---

## Two ways to get it

- **OData connector type.** Pick *OData* when creating a connector. Choose *SAP Gateway* for an SAP system (the base URL is the host, e.g. `https://s4.example.com:44300`, services come from SAP's catalog), or leave it off for a single OData service (the base URL is the service root, e.g. `https://services.example.com/odata/v4/Sales`).
- **A REST connector with OData settings.** A REST connector whose `config.odata` is set gets the same built-in tools; its own tools stay plain REST calls. The SAP S/4HANA Cloud catalog adapter works this way.

Both use the REST engine underneath, so every REST authentication method applies (Basic, OAuth 2.0 client credentials or authorization code, API key, certificates, login token), as do retries, the outbound SSRF guard and the proxy.

## Built-in tools

Every OData connector carries five tools, named `<prefix>_…` (the prefix is the connector name plus `_odata`, or `config.odata.toolPrefix`):

| Tool | What it does |
|------|--------------|
| `<prefix>_list_services` | SAP: searches the Gateway service catalog, V2 (`/IWFND/CATALOGSERVICE`) and V4 (service groups), cached for an hour. Otherwise: the services listed in the connector's settings, or the single service root. |
| `<prefix>_describe_service` | Entity sets with their labels, keys, number of fields, and flags: *analytical* (the server aggregates), *parameters* (parameterised view), *requiredInFilter*, *readOnly*. `$metadata` is cached for 24 hours; `refresh: true` reloads it. |
| `<prefix>_describe_entity` | Every field with label, type, key, the currency/unit field (`sap:unit`, `Measures.ISOCurrency`), the text field (`sap:text`, `Common.Text`), filterable/sortable and dimension/measure role; navigation properties; hints for analytical and parameterised sets. |
| `<prefix>_query` | `select`, `filter`, `orderby`, `top` (≤ 1000), `skip`, `expand`, `parameters`, V4 `apply` and `search`. Field names are checked against the model first ("Unknown field … Did you mean …"), required filters are enforced, server paging is followed on the connector's own host only, and the answer is flattened: plain rows, dates as ISO strings, decimals as strings, total count and `nextSkip`. |
| `<prefix>_get_entity` | One entity by key; a composite key as `{"SalesOrder": "1", "SalesOrderItem": "10"}`. |

The built-ins only read, and are annotated read-only for MCP clients.

## Settings (`config.odata`)

| Key | Meaning |
|-----|---------|
| `sap` | SAP Gateway mode: catalog discovery, SAP parameters. Implied by `sapClient`. |
| `sapClient` | Three-digit SAP client, sent as `sap-client` on every request. |
| `sapLanguage` | Sent as `sap-language`, e.g. `EN`. |
| `services` | Allowed service paths, `*` as wildcard. Other services are refused. Without wildcards, the list is also what `list_services` returns on a non-SAP connector. |
| `version` | `v2` or `v4` to override detection from `$metadata`. |
| `maxRows` | Row cap per query, at most 1000. |
| `toolPrefix` | Prefix of the built-in tool names. |

All of them can hold `{{VARIABLES}}`, resolved from the connector's environment variables at call time. They are edited under the connector's settings.

## Importing tools from `$metadata`

**Import Tools → OData $metadata** turns a service's entity sets into named tools: `<set>_list` (with filter, select, orderby, top, skip, expand) and `<set>_get` (key parameters). Give the service path (SAP) or leave it empty (single service); the document is fetched with the connector's credentials. You can also paste a `$metadata` document and limit the import to some entity sets. Re-importing a service updates its tools and retires only that service's tools that disappeared, never the built-ins or another service's tools.

On an OData connector, imported and hand-written HTTP tools get the SAP client and language, JSON format for V2 and flattened answers. SAP writes (POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE) fetch a CSRF token with the session cookies first.

## SAP Gateway setup

1. A technical user of type *System*, with a productive password, in the client you want to read.
2. A role with `S_SERVICE` for the services the agent may call, and display-only business authorizations. For catalog browsing, also the V2 catalog service `/IWFND/CATALOGSERVICE` and the V4 catalog. SAP checks these authorizations on every call; they are the real boundary.
3. Active services (`/IWFND/MAINT_SERVICE`, `/IWFND/V4_ADMIN`).
4. Network: the Gateway port is usually internal. Self-host AnythingMCP inside the network or reach it through a VPN, and add the host to `SSRF_ALLOWED_HOSTS`.

SAP's API policy expects third-party integrations to use published APIs (`API_*` services on the SAP Business Accelerator Hub) or services the customer built; restrict `services` accordingly.

The **SAP S/4HANA (OData)** catalog adapter packages all of this for on-premise and Private Cloud systems: the built-ins with the `s4` prefix, ready tools for journal entry items, billing documents, sales orders, business partners, material stock and products, and a guide (`s4_guide`) to filters, analytical services and KPIs.

---

## docs/connectors/per-user-sign-in.md

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HelpCode-ai/anythingmcp/main/docs/connectors/per-user-sign-in.md

# Per-user sign-in for OAuth2 connectors

> Needs **AnythingMCP Enterprise**. Available on AnythingMCP Cloud and on
> self-hosted instances with an Enterprise licence key. The 30-day trial does
> not include it.

By default an OAuth2 connector is authorized **once**: whoever clicks
"Authorize with Provider" signs in, and every user of the workspace then calls
the provider with that one account. Everyone sees what that account can see.

With **per-user sign-in**, every user connects **their own** account. Each tool
call carries the token the provider issued to the caller, so the provider's own
permissions decide what each user sees and may change. This suits providers that
already govern access per user: a remote MCP server such as mfr's, or Microsoft
365, Google and similar APIs.

## Turning it on

1. Open the connector. It must use **OAuth2** with a browser sign-in
   (authorization code). API keys, passwords and the client-credentials grant
   stay shared: there is no user to sign in.
2. In the **Sign-in** card, the connector's owner or an admin clicks
   **Require each user to sign in (Enterprise)** and confirms.
3. Every user connects their own account: on the connector page in the
   dashboard (**Connect my account**), or on the connect page (below). Either
   way they then sign in at the provider with their own account.

Switching to per-user removes the authorization stored on the connector. The OAuth
client stays: the client ID and secret, and on MCP servers the dynamically
registered client. Switching back to a shared sign-in removes every user's own
sign-in, and the connector then needs one authorization of its own again.

## The connect page

Every per-user connector also has a connect page at
`<FRONTEND_URL>/auth/connect/<connector id>`. It is served by the backend next
to the sign-in page MCP clients open, so it works wherever MCP sign-in works,
also on a self-hosted server whose dashboard is not reachable from outside.
Send your team this link, or let the model hand it over: the error of a call
without a sign-in links to it.

On the page a user:

1. signs in to AnythingMCP, with the workspace's identity provider (Microsoft
   Entra ID or another OIDC provider set up under **Settings → Identity
   providers**), or with the dashboard session already open in that browser;
2. clicks **Connect my account** and signs in at the provider;
3. is back on the page, connected.

Without an identity provider (and on AnythingMCP Cloud) the page sends users to
the connector in the dashboard instead.

What the page guards:

- The sign-in there is valid for 15 minutes and for `/auth/connect` only. It
  is not a dashboard session. **Sign out everywhere** ends it.
- The tokens go to the user signed in on the page, and only in the browser that
  started the connection. A provider link forwarded to someone else, or opened
  in another browser, stores nothing.
- Before signing in, the page names no connector, so a link reveals nothing to
  someone outside the workspace.

Behind a reverse proxy, `/auth/` and `/api/mcp-oauth/` must reach the backend,
and so must the identity provider's redirect URI `<FRONTEND_URL>/auth/sso/callback`.
These are the same routes MCP sign-in and the connector's OAuth callback
already use.

## What each call does

- **The caller's own sign-in.** A call uses the token of the signed-in user who
  makes it, from an MCP client or from **Run Test** and **Test connection** in
  the dashboard. The connector's own token is never used, so a missing sign-in
  never falls back to someone else's.
- **Not connected yet.** The call fails before anything is sent. The error names
  the connector and links to its connect page, so the model can tell the user
  where to connect.
- **No signed-in user.** A call that does not come from a user fails the same
  way, for example a workspace API key or a job that runs on its own.
- **Response cache.** For tools with a response cache, entries are kept per user.
  One user's cached answer is never served to another.

## Expired or refused sign-ins

Tokens refresh automatically for each user, under that user's own refresh lock.
When the provider refuses a user's refresh token, for example after a password
change, a revocation or a long period of inactivity, the sign-in is marked
**Your sign-in expired** for that user only. That user gets one email, and their
calls fail at once with what to do. Other users are not affected. Connecting
again, on the connect page that the email links to or on the connector page,
clears it.

When the OAuth client itself stops working, for example because a client secret
expired, every user's sign-in fails. The connector's OAuth settings need
fixing, and each user then signs in again.

## Tools of an MCP connector

The tools of a per-user MCP connector are imported when users sign in, with the
first user's account and with each later sign-in. **Re-discover Tools** lists
them with your own sign-in. The remote server still checks every call against the
caller's own permissions.

## API

| Method and path | Who | What |
|---|---|---|
| `PATCH /api/connectors/:id/credential-scope` `{ "credentialScope": "USER" \| "SHARED" }` | owner or admin | Switch the mode (USER needs Enterprise) |
| `POST /api/connectors/:id/oauth/authorize` | any member (per-user connectors) | Start your own sign-in |
| `GET /api/connectors/:id/my-credential` | any member | Whether you are connected; no token is returned |
| `DELETE /api/connectors/:id/my-credential` | any member | Disconnect your own account |
| `GET /auth/connect/:id` | anyone (HTML) | The connect page; signs the user in first |

Tokens are stored encrypted with `ENCRYPTION_KEY`, one row per user and
connector (`user_connector_credentials`). They are deleted with the user, the
connector or the workspace. Connector exports never include them.
