## docs/tool-definition.md

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HelpCode-ai/anythingmcp/main/docs/tool-definition.md

# Tool Definition Format

> How to define MCP tools in AnythingMCP: parameters, endpoint mapping, and response mapping.

[Back to README](<https://github.com/HelpCode-ai/anythingmcp/blob/main/README.md>)

---

## Overview

Every MCP tool in AnythingMCP is defined by three JSON objects:

1. **`parameters`** — What the AI can pass as input (JSON Schema)
2. **`endpointMapping`** — How parameters map to the API request
3. **`responseMapping`** — (Optional) How to transform the API response

## Adapter envelope

The catalog validator requires each adapter to provide `slug`, `name`,
`description`, `region`, `category`, `icon`, `docsUrl`, `requiredEnvVars`,
`connector`, and a non-empty `tools` array. The filename must match `slug`.
Optional environment variables use the same array-of-strings shape and must
not duplicate a required variable.

### Adapter fields

Keep the required envelope fields above at the adapter root; use arrays for
`requiredEnvVars` and `optionalEnvVars`, and do not list one variable in both.

When a variable is renamed, list its previous names under `envVarAliases`,
keyed by the current name: `{ "IS24_CONSUMER_KEY": ["IS24_CLIENT_ID"] }`.
Connectors installed before the rename still hold the old name; saving their
environment variables reads it when the current one is not set, instead of
leaving an unresolved `{{IS24_CONSUMER_KEY}}` in the credentials.

`aliases` lists other names people search the app by: a former name
(`["lexoffice"]` for Lexware Office), a translation (`"Mercado Livre"`), a
common short form (`"D365"`, `"SAP B1"`) or the vendor's umbrella brand
(`"Facebook"` on Meta Ads, Instagram and WhatsApp). The catalog search in the
store, on /welcome and in the chat matches them like the name; they are never
displayed. Keep them to names that clearly mean this app, each at most 40
characters; a misspelling needs no alias, the search tolerates typos.

`envVarMeta.<VAR>.pattern` (with `patternMessage`) is enforced on every path
that writes the variable: the setup form, the pre-save check, the install
(also "Save anyway" and a chat install) and the connector's variable editor.
Those paths also refuse, field by field, an address or credential still
holding an example (`host`, `example.com`, `your-api-key`, `<...>`,
`PASTE_KEY_HERE`) and a credential pasted more than once (the same string
repeated). See `packages/backend/src/adapters/env-var-checks.ts`.

`envVarMeta.<VAR>.options` gives a variable a fixed list of choices, for an
API with one host per country or region. The setup form shows a select with
the labels instead of a text field, a model setting the connector up from a
chat is given the list and asks the user to pick, and every path that writes
the variable refuses a value that is not one of the listed `value`s (an
optional variable may stay empty). List 2 to 20 choices with unique values;
write each `value` exactly as it is stored (a whole `https://` URL when the
variable starts `connector.baseUrl`), make it match `pattern` when there is
one, and never combine `options` with `"secret": true`:

```json
"envVarMeta": {
  "ACME_MARKET_URL": {
    "label": "Country",
    "kind": "address",
    "help": "The country of your seller account.",
    "options": [
      { "value": "https://fr.market.example.com", "label": "France" },
      { "value": "https://es.market.example.com", "label": "Spain" }
    ]
  }
}
```

`verifyHints` maps a status (`"401"`) or failure kind (`"auth_failed"`,
`"unreachable"`) to what the setup check tells the user. A tool call that
the API answers 401 uses the adapter's `"401"` (or `"auth_failed"`) hint too
when no built-in rule matches, followed by a link to the connector's page,
so a connector saved without a passing check hears the same advice. Hints are
read from the catalog at call time and reach installed connectors without
"Apply update". Declare a `probe` (a read call with fixed `params`) when no
GET without required parameters exists; without one the setup check is
skipped and a wrong key is only found at the first call. An adapter for a
vendor's MCP server (`connector.type` `MCP`) without a `probe` is checked by
listing the server's tools, which catches a refused token. A hint written as
`{ "hint": "…", "field": "VAR" }` is also shown under that variable on the
setup form.

A probe can still fail when the call answers: an MCP tool result with
`isError: true` fails the check, and `probe.failWhen` lists answers that mean
the connector cannot work although nothing was refused. Each rule's `matches`
is a case-insensitive regular expression over the answer's text (for an MCP
tool, the text of its result); the first match fails the check with its
`hint`, under `field` when it names one, as `kind` (default `auth_failed`):

```json
"probe": {
  "tool": "atlassian_discover",
  "params": { "query": "get issue details" },
  "failWhen": [
    {
      "matches": "missing the scope claim|\"searchableProducts\"\\s*:\\s*\\[\\s*\\]",
      "hint": "This API token has no scopes. Create an 'API token with scopes' …",
      "field": "ATLASSIAN_API_TOKEN"
    }
  ]
}
```

`derivedEnvVars` declares settings the user should not have to look up,
found at setup from a host they do know. Each entry names the variable that
holds the host (`fromHost`, declared in `optionalEnvVars` or
`requiredEnvVars`), a public `url` starting with `https://{{<fromHost>}}/`,
the dotted `path` of the value in its JSON answer, an optional `pattern` the
value must match, and the `error` shown under the host field when the host
answers without a value (`{{host}}` is replaced by it). The host is stored as
a bare lower-case host (`https://Acme.atlassian.net/` becomes
`acme.atlassian.net`). The lookup runs at the setup check, at install and in
the connector's variable editor when the host changes; when the host does not
answer at all (timeout, 5xx), the connector is saved without the value. See
`packages/backend/src/adapters/derived-settings.ts`:

```json
"derivedEnvVars": {
  "ATLASSIAN_CLOUD_ID": {
    "fromHost": "ATLASSIAN_SITE",
    "url": "https://{{ATLASSIAN_SITE}}/_edge/tenant_info",
    "path": "cloudId",
    "pattern": "^[0-9a-fA-F-]{36}$",
    "error": "No Atlassian site answers at {{host}}."
  }
}
```

`instructionFacts` are sentences added to a catalog connector's instructions
when they are served to a model (initialize, the workspace guide), each only
when every `{{VAR}}` it names is set on the connector. Only non-secret
variables (declared or derived) may be named. Stored instructions never
resolve `{{VAR}}`, so this is how a per-workspace fact (the Atlassian site and
its cloudId) reaches the model. Facts are read from the catalog when the
instructions are served and reach installed connectors without "Apply
update". See `packages/backend/src/adapters/instruction-facts.ts`.

### Tools

Each entry in `tools` needs a string `name`, a useful `description`, and its
JSON-Schema `parameters` when it accepts input. Parameter properties should
include descriptions for the model. `"enabled": false` installs a tool switched
off, for writes a workspace should turn on deliberately.

See [connector configuration](<https://github.com/HelpCode-ai/anythingmcp/blob/main/docs/tool-definition.md#connector>)
and [authentication](<https://github.com/HelpCode-ai/anythingmcp/blob/main/docs/tool-definition.md#authentication>) for the nested connector fields.

### Connector

Set `connector.type` to `REST`, `GRAPHQL`, `SOAP`, `MCP`, `DATABASE`, or
`LOGIN_TOKEN`. Set `connector.authType` to a supported authentication scheme
listed below; these values are validated before an adapter can pass.

### Errors inside a 200 response

Some APIs answer every request with HTTP 200 and report a failure in the body:
PeopleHR returns `{"Status": 5, "Message": "API Key does not exists."}`, Korea's
law.go.kr returns `{"result": "사용자 정보 검증에 실패하였습니다.", "msg": "..."}`.
Without help such a call counts as a success: the install check passes with a
wrong key and the model has to spot the refusal itself. A REST adapter can
describe its error shape in `connector.config.errorWhen`, one rule or a list:

```json
"connector": {
  "type": "REST",
  "config": {
    "errorWhen": [
      { "path": "Status", "in": [1, 2], "messagePath": "Message", "status": 401 },
      { "path": "Status", "equals": 5, "messagePath": "Message", "messageMatches": "API Key does not exist|Access Denied", "status": 401 },
      { "path": "Status", "in": [3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9], "messagePath": "Message", "status": 400 },
      { "path": "Status", "equals": 6, "messagePath": "Message", "status": 502 }
    ]
  }
}
```

| Field | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `path` | Dotted path into the parsed body (`Status`, `error.code`, `errors[0].code`). Required. |
| `equals` | The value equals this one. Scalars compare as text, so `5` also matches `"5"`. |
| `in` | The value is one of these. |
| `matches` | The value, as text, matches this case-insensitive regular expression. |
| _(none of the three)_ | The field is present and not `null`, `false`, `""` or `0`. |
| `messagePath` | Where the error text is; a list is joined with a space. Defaults to the value at `path`. |
| `messageMatches` | The rule only applies when the error text also matches this regular expression. |
| `status` | The status the failure reports, which decides how it is classified: 401/403 `auth_failed`, 400/422 `bad_request`, 404 `not_found`, 429 `rate_limited`, 5xx `upstream_error`. Default `400`. |

Rules are checked in order and the first match wins, so put the specific ones
(an auth message) before the general ones. A match turns the response into a
failed tool call carrying the API's text and the whole body; the install probe,
Verify and the tool test in the dashboard classify it by `status`. JSON-RPC
error envelopes (`{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "error": {...}}`) are recognised without a
rule. Connectors installed from the catalog follow the adapter's rules even if
they were installed before the rules existed; a connector's own
`config.errorWhen` overrides them, and `[]` switches the check off.

### Authentication

Use `NONE`, `API_KEY`, `BEARER_TOKEN`, `BASIC`, `BASIC_AUTH`, `OAUTH2`,
`OAUTH1`, `LOGIN_TOKEN`, `QUERY_AUTH`, `CONNECTION_STRING` or `HMAC` as
`connector.authType`. Keep the corresponding credentials in `authConfig` and
reference environment variables with `{{VAR}}` where the connector injects
them.

For `OAUTH2`, `authConfig.tokenAuthMethod` says how the client authenticates
at the token endpoint: `client_secret_post` (default), `client_secret_basic`,
or `private_key_jwt`, which signs a short-lived client assertion with a private
key instead of sending a secret (see
[REST connectors](<https://github.com/HelpCode-ai/anythingmcp/blob/main/docs/connectors/rest.md#signed-client-assertion-private_key_jwt>)).

The browser sign-in ("Authorize with Provider") sends this server's callback
URL (`<SERVER_URL>/api/mcp-oauth/callback`) as `redirect_uri`. A provider that
wants something else there names it in `authConfig.providerRedirectUri`, which
is then sent on the authorization request and on the code exchange alike.
eBay is the case: its `redirect_uri` is the app's RuName, and the RuName's
"Auth Accepted URL" in eBay's developer portal points at the callback URL.
Use a variable (`"providerRedirectUri": "{{EBAY_RUNAME}}"`); until it has a
value, the sign-in asks for it instead of starting. `authConfig.pkce: false`
leaves out the PKCE challenge and verifier for providers that do not use them.

A `User-Agent` set for the API calls, in `authConfig.extraHeaders` or in the
connector's `headers` (`extraHeaders` wins, as it does on the API calls), is
also sent on the token requests: the authorization-code exchange, refreshes
and client-credentials grants. Reddit throttles generic agents at its token
endpoint as well. No other header is forwarded there.

### HMAC-signed requests

Some APIs never receive the secret: each request carries a digest computed
over a canonical string. `authType: "HMAC"` describes that string in the
adapter rather than in per-vendor engine code. Signing happens after the body
and query are built, because the canonical string usually folds them in.

```json
"authType": "HMAC",
"authConfig": {
  "signature": {
    "algorithm": "sha256",
    "encoding": "hex",
    "secret": "{{KAUFLAND_SECRET_KEY}}",
    "template": "${method}\n${url}\n${body}\n${timestamp}\n",
    "headerName": "Shop-Signature",
    "timestampHeader": "Shop-Timestamp",
    "extraHeaders": { "Shop-Client-Key": "{{KAUFLAND_CLIENT_KEY}}" }
  }
}
```

`template` may use `${method}`, `${url}`, `${path}` (path + query only),
`${body}` and `${timestamp}` (Unix seconds), in whatever order the vendor
documents. `\n` is honoured. `algorithm` is `sha256` (default), `sha1` or
`sha512`; `encoding` is `hex` (default) or `base64`. `timestampHeader` sends
the same timestamp that went into the string, which the server needs to
recompute it.

The body is signed exactly as it will be sent — signing a different rendering
of the same object is the usual way an HMAC integration fails with an error
that blames the key.

#### Signed JWT per request (opt-in)

Some APIs want a short-lived JWT signed with a shared secret on every request
instead of a digest (Ghost's Admin API). A `jwt` block in `signature` switches
to that: a fresh token is signed for each call and each retry, so the
connector stores only the key, never a token that expires.

```json
"authType": "HMAC",
"authConfig": {
  "signature": {
    "jwt": {
      "key": "{{GHOST_ADMIN_API_KEY}}",
      "keyFormat": "id:secret",
      "secretEncoding": "hex",
      "algorithm": "HS256",
      "ttlSeconds": 300,
      "claims": { "aud": "/admin/" }
    },
    "headerName": "Authorization",
    "headerTemplate": "Ghost ${jwt}"
  }
}
```

| Field | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `jwt.key` + `jwt.keyFormat` | One `<id>:<secret>` value: the id becomes the `kid` header, the secret signs. `id:secret` is the only format. |
| `jwt.keyId`, `jwt.secret` | The same two parts as separate values, instead of `key`. `keyId` is optional. |
| `jwt.secretEncoding` | How the secret turns into key bytes: `utf8` (default), `hex` or `base64`. |
| `jwt.algorithm` | `HS256` (default), `HS384` or `HS512`. |
| `jwt.ttlSeconds` | Token lifetime, default 300, at most 3600. |
| `jwt.claims` | Claims added to the payload (`aud`, `iss`, …). `iat` and `exp` are always set by the engine. |
| `headerName` | Default `Authorization`. |
| `headerTemplate` | `${jwt}` is the token. Default `Bearer ${jwt}`. |

`extraHeaders` are sent as with a digest signature. Errors name the field that
is wrong (no colon in the key, a secret that is not hex, an unset variable) and
never include the key.

#### Query signing (opt-in)

Some platforms put the digest and the timestamp in the query instead of a
header. These fields switch to that path; a signature without any of them is
computed exactly as described above.

| Field | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `placement` | `header` (default) or `query`: the digest goes into the query parameter `paramName`. |
| `paramName` | Name of that query parameter, default `sign`. |
| `timestampParam` | Sends the timestamp as this query parameter. |
| `timestampFormat` | `s` (default, Unix seconds), `ms` (milliseconds) or `iso` (ISO 8601 in UTC, `2026-11-06T07:00:00+00:00`), for `${timestamp}`, `timestampParam` and `timestampHeader` alike. |
| `queryParams` | Static query parameters added to every call (an app key, a fixed `sign_method`), signed like the others. |
| `encoding` | Also `hex-upper`: hex in capitals. |
| `excludeMultipartBody` | `true`: `${body}` is empty when the body is `multipart/form-data` (file uploads), for vendors that sign uploads without their body. |

On this path the template may also use:

- `${pathname}`: the URL path without the query.
- `${apiPath}`: the path below the connector's `baseUrl`, without the query
  (`/auth/token/create` when `baseUrl` is `https://api-sg.aliexpress.com/rest`).
- `${query.NAME}`: the value of one query parameter as sent, empty when absent.
- `${sortedParams}`: every parameter sent, sorted by name (ASCII order) and
  concatenated as name + value with no separators. It covers the query as sent,
  including `queryParams`, the timestamp and parameters a token provider adds,
  and the fields of an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` body. An array or
  object contributes the same pairs the query serializer sends for it
  (`ids=1&ids=2`, `page[size]=20`). The signature parameter itself and empty
  values are left out.
- `${sortedQuery}`: the query parameters as sent (no body), sorted by name and
  written as `name=value` pairs joined with `&`, names and values
  percent-encoded per RFC 3986 (only `A-Z a-z 0-9 - . _ ~` unescaped). The
  signature parameter is left out; empty values are kept, because they are
  sent. This is the Rocket SellerCenter signature (Falabella Seller Center).

Variables are replaced in one pass, so a value that contains `${body}` is
signed as that literal text. Shopee (`intl/shopee.json`) signs
`${query.partner_id}${pathname}${timestamp}...`. The Alibaba IOP gateways
(AliExpress, see `intl/aliexpress-affiliate.json`) sign every parameter:

```json
"signature": {
  "algorithm": "sha256",
  "encoding": "hex-upper",
  "secret": "{{ALIEXPRESS_APP_SECRET}}",
  "placement": "query",
  "paramName": "sign",
  "timestampParam": "timestamp",
  "timestampFormat": "ms",
  "queryParams": { "app_key": "{{ALIEXPRESS_APP_KEY}}", "sign_method": "sha256" },
  "template": "${sortedParams}"
}
```

Their `/sync?method=...` business calls sign `${sortedParams}` (the `method`
parameter is one of them); calls on their `/rest` gateway put the API path in
front: `${apiPath}${sortedParams}`. JSON-valued parameters go in a form body
with the `__json` marker, which `${sortedParams}` signs as its JSON text.

Falabella Seller Center (`intl/falabella-seller-center.json`) signs the
sorted query with the user's API key and sends it as `Signature`, with an ISO
8601 `Timestamp`:

```json
"signature": {
  "algorithm": "sha256",
  "encoding": "hex",
  "secret": "{{FALABELLA_API_KEY}}",
  "placement": "query",
  "paramName": "Signature",
  "timestampParam": "Timestamp",
  "timestampFormat": "iso",
  "queryParams": { "UserID": "{{FALABELLA_USER_ID}}", "Version": "1.0", "Format": "JSON" },
  "template": "${sortedQuery}"
}
```

TikTok Shop (`intl/tiktok-shop.json`) wraps the path, the sorted query and the
body in the app secret: `{{SECRET}}${pathname}${sortedParams}${body}{{SECRET}}`,
with `queryParams: { "app_key": ... }` and `excludeMultipartBody: true`. Pass
array values as comma-separated strings on this kind of adapter: TikTok signs
one value per query key.

#### Shop authorization (token providers)

Two marketplaces authorize a shop with their own flow instead of OAuth 2, set
with `authConfig.tokenProvider` on an `HMAC` connector. The provider stores the
shop's tokens encrypted on the connector, renews them before they expire, adds
them to every call, and marks the connector as needing a new authorization when
the marketplace refuses the refresh token. The connector page shows
**Authorize with Provider** until the shop is authorized.

| `tokenProvider` | Flow | What it adds to each call |
|-----------------|------|---------------------------|
| `shopee` | Signed `auth_partner` link; callback `<SERVER_URL>/api/shopee/callback/<state>` | `access_token` and `shop_id` query parameters, signed |
| `tiktok-shop` | `services.tiktokshop.com/open/authorize?service_id=...` (US: `services.us.tiktokshop.com`); callback `<SERVER_URL>/api/tiktok-shop/callback`, set as the app's Redirect URL | the access token in the `x-tts-access-token` header (not signed) and `shop_cipher` in the query (signed), except on `/authorization/`, `/seller/` and upload paths |

The TikTok Shop provider reads the app key from `authConfig.appKey` (or the
`app_key` query parameter), the secret from `signature.secret` and the Service
ID from `authConfig.serviceId`. The optional connector variables
`TIKTOK_SHOP_MARKET` (`US`) and `TIKTOK_SHOP_SHOP_ID` (shop id, code or name,
when one authorization covers several shops) are read when the authorization
starts and completes.

When the server sets `TIKTOK_SHOP_PLATFORM_APP_KEY`,
`TIKTOK_SHOP_PLATFORM_APP_SECRET` and `TIKTOK_SHOP_PLATFORM_SERVICE_ID` (a
public TikTok Shop App Store app), a connector whose app key resolves empty
uses that app instead: the provider fills `appKey`, `serviceId`,
`signature.secret`, the signed `app_key` and the template
`<secret>${pathname}${sortedParams}${body}<secret>` in memory for each call,
authorization and renewal, and never writes them to the connector. That is why
the adapter's `TIKTOK_SHOP_APP_KEY`, `TIKTOK_SHOP_APP_SECRET` and
`TIKTOK_SHOP_SERVICE_ID` are optional variables: saved empty, they ask for the
server's app. On a server without one, the setup check still reports them as
missing. A callback that carries a code but no state (an install from the
App Store, `?app_key=...&code=...&shop_region=...`) is kept as a single-use
install record for 30 minutes when its `app_key` is the server's; the
dashboard completes it with `POST /api/tiktok-shop/install` once the seller is
signed in, reusing the workspace's newest TikTok Shop connector that uses the
server's app and has no shop authorized yet, or installing a new one.

#### Meta sign-in (Instagram connectors)

Meta's logins issue no refresh token, so the two Instagram adapters stay
`BEARER_TOKEN` connectors with `authConfig.tokenRenewal` and get their token
from a sign-in instead of a paste. The connector page and the setup page show
**Authorize with Provider**. The callback is `<SERVER_URL>/api/meta/callback`
for every flavour (`meta-auth.controller.ts`, `meta-login.util.ts`):

- `instagram` with an app that has a Unified Login configuration id
  (`META_CONFIG_ID`, or the server's `META_PLATFORM_CONFIG_ID`): the dialog
  takes `config_id` instead of `scope`, the user signs in with Instagram or
  Facebook and shares a business portfolio's Instagram accounts. The code
  gives a Business Integration System User token that does not expire; it is
  stored as is and never renewed. `/me/assigned_instagram_accounts` lists the
  accounts. Meta apps created since autumn 2026 only offer this login.
- `instagram` with an older app (no configuration id): classic Facebook Login
  with a `scope` list; the code is exchanged for a long-lived user token
  (`fb_exchange_token`) and the account comes from the user's Pages.
- `instagram-login`: Instagram Login (`ig_exchange_token`), for apps that
  still have it; always the connector's own app.

The completion writes the token to `INSTAGRAM_ACCESS_TOKEN` and the account
id to `INSTAGRAM_ACCOUNT_ID` (several accounts: the user picks one), rebuilds
the stored bearer token as the variable editor does and hands the expiry to
the bearer token renewal. Pasting a token keeps working.

The app comes from the connector (`META_APP_ID` / `META_APP_SECRET` /
`META_CONFIG_ID`, or `INSTAGRAM_APP_ID` / `INSTAGRAM_APP_SECRET`), else, for
`instagram` only, from the server (`META_PLATFORM_APP_ID` / `_SECRET` /
`META_PLATFORM_CONFIG_ID`), the same on Cloud and self-hosted. A user token
issued through the server's classic Facebook Login app is renewed with that
app; a pasted token never is. Deleting a connector deletes its tool-call log
rows with it (they cascade with its tools), so no Instagram data outlives the
connector. The flavour is chosen by the connector's catalog adapter
(`meta-login.util.ts`), so a new Meta adapter that should sign in this way is
added there.

### MCP adapters (a vendor's own MCP server)

When a vendor already runs an official MCP server, the adapter bridges it
instead of describing its API again. `connector.type` is `MCP`, `baseUrl` is
the server's MCP endpoint (variables allowed, e.g.
`https://{{SPLUNK_HOST}}:8089/services/mcp`), and authentication is whatever
the server accepts (usually `BEARER_TOKEN`).

At install AnythingMCP asks that server for its tools (`tools/list`) and
installs what it lists, so a workspace gets exactly the tools of the server
version it runs. The adapter's `tools` array is a snapshot: it is what the
catalog shows, the fallback installed when the server cannot be reached at
install, and the place for policy. A snapshot tool with `"enabled": false`
installs switched off, and `annotations` set there fill the hints the server
leaves out (the server's own hints win). `omitParameters` (an array of
top-level parameter names) drops those parameters from the schema the server
lists, at install and on every **Discover tools**, for vendor fields such as
attribution that a workspace has no use for.
Each tool's `endpointMapping` is `{ "method": "<remote tool name>", "path": "/mcp" }`
(`"/"` for a server at the root of its host, together with
`connector.config.mcpPath: "/"`).
Listing the tools is also the install check, so no `probe` is needed, and a
catalog update never rewrites or retires the tools of an MCP adapter: the
server owns them. See `intl/splunk.json` and `intl/linear.json`.

Set `connector.config.mcpToolPrefix` (e.g. `"linear_"`) so the tools do not
collide with another bridge's on the same MCP server: the snapshot's `name` is
then the prefixed local name and `endpointMapping.method` the remote one. An
adapter that signs in at the provider uses `authType: "OAUTH2"` with no
`authConfig`; `connector.config.mcpOAuth` says how (dynamic registration,
a client of the user's own from `{{VAR}}`s, scope, RFC 8707 resource). Both
are described in [MCP Bridge](<https://github.com/HelpCode-ai/anythingmcp/blob/main/docs/connectors/mcp-bridge.md#connector-settings-connectorconfig>).
`prerequisites` (an array of short sentences) lists what the user needs at
the vendor first; the setup page shows it above the form.
`requiresIpAllowlist: true` marks an API that refuses every call from an
address not registered with the provider (eMAG, Shopee, the Korean law API):
the setup page then shows the server's outbound IP addresses (`EGRESS_IPS`)
as a step to complete, not as a side note.

### DATABASE adapters

A `DATABASE` adapter points at a database instead of an HTTP API, so several
of the REST rules simply do not apply to it:

- `authType` is `CONNECTION_STRING`. `baseUrl` is the DSN and carries the
  driver (`postgres://`, `mysql://`, `mariadb://`, `mssql://`, `oracle://`,
  `mongodb://`, `sqlite://`) — the engine picks the driver from that prefix.
- Put the username and password in `authConfig`, not in the DSN. `authConfig`
  is encrypted at rest; `baseUrl` is not. The engine splices them into the URL
  (Postgres, MySQL, Mongo) or passes them as driver config (MSSQL, Oracle,
  which also accept `authConfig.domain` for NTLM).
- `endpointMapping.method` is `query`, `static`, or `mongo_schema` — never an
  HTTP verb. `path` is the statement, not a URL.
- A `path` of exactly `${query}` hands the engine the caller's raw SQL. Any
  other `path` is a template whose `${name}` placeholders are compiled to
  bound parameters, never string-interpolated.
- Adapters install **read-only**; the engine rejects anything but a read until
  the user flips the switch in the connector's settings.
- Declare a `probe` (a listing tool with no required parameters). A DATABASE
  adapter has no HTTP healthcheck, so without one the install reports nothing.

```json
{
  "slug": "postgres",
  "requiredEnvVars": ["POSTGRES_HOST", "POSTGRES_PORT", "POSTGRES_DATABASE", "POSTGRES_USER", "POSTGRES_PASSWORD"],
  "probe": { "tool": "postgres_list_tables" },
  "connector": {
    "name": "PostgreSQL",
    "type": "DATABASE",
    "authType": "CONNECTION_STRING",
    "baseUrl": "postgres://{{POSTGRES_HOST}}:{{POSTGRES_PORT}}/{{POSTGRES_DATABASE}}",
    "authConfig": {
      "username": "{{POSTGRES_USER}}",
      "password": "{{POSTGRES_PASSWORD}}"
    }
  },
  "tools": [
    {
      "name": "postgres_query",
      "description": "Run a read-only SQL SELECT against the database and return up to 1000 rows.",
      "parameters": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": { "query": { "type": "string", "description": "A single SQL SELECT statement." } },
        "required": ["query"]
      },
      "endpointMapping": { "method": "query", "path": "${query}" }
    }
  ]
}
```

### Setup guide

`setupGuide` turns the setup page into a step-by-step guide: an intro (what
the AI can do with the app, what to have ready, why the setup works the way it
does), then one step at a time, then the connector link and the steps to use
it in Claude, ChatGPT or Copilot. Add one where the plain form is not enough:
an app of the user's own (Etsy), a bot to create (Telegram), keys found three
menus deep. Adapters without one keep the form.

```json
"setupGuide": {
  "effort": "own_app",
  "minutes": 10,
  "examples": ["Which orders have not shipped yet?"],
  "needs": ["Your Etsy seller account"],
  "why": "Etsy lets other tools reach a shop only through an app its owner registers.",
  "steps": [
    {
      "id": "callback",
      "title": "Add the callback URL",
      "body": "Open your app and add this address under **Callback URLs**.",
      "action": { "label": "Open your Etsy apps", "url": "https://www.etsy.com/developers/your-apps" },
      "values": [{ "label": "Callback URL", "value": "{{redirectUri}}" }],
      "confirm": "I added the callback URL and saved",
      "problems": [{ "q": "Etsy says the redirect URI is wrong", "a": "Paste it again, exactly." }]
    },
    { "id": "keys", "title": "Copy your keys", "fields": ["ETSY_CLIENT_ID", "ETSY_CLIENT_SECRET"] }
  ]
}
```

- `effort`: `none`, `one_click`, `api_key`, `own_app` or `admin_needed`; with
  `minutes` it is the badge on the marketplace card. Without a guide the
  badge is derived from how the adapter signs in.
- `values`: what to type or pick on the provider's page, each with a copy
  button (`"pick": true` for an option to select, without one). Only
  `{{redirectUri}}` is filled in: the OAuth callback URL of the instance.
- `fields`: the variables entered in that step. Every required variable that
  is not `advanced` is asked for in exactly one step; the last step checks
  them against the API and installs (or sends the user to the provider's
  sign-in), so put the fields there or before it.
- `image`: a real screenshot under `packages/frontend/public`, with `alt` and
  `capturedAt`. Leave it out rather than add a mock-up.
- `confirm`: a checkbox the user ticks before continuing, for a step that
  happens at the provider.
- `saveAndCheck: true`: for a provider that must approve the user's app
  before the keys work (Etsy). Continue saves the step's `fields` on the
  connector (unfinished, so the AI cannot use it yet) and asks the provider
  about the keys with the adapter's `checkBeforeAuthorization`. Needs
  `fields`, and cannot be the last step.
- `waitForProvider: true`: the step right after a `saveAndCheck` step, shown
  only while the provider refuses the saved keys and skipped once it accepts
  them. It tells the user what they are waiting for; the page checks again
  whenever they come back to it and offers "Check again", and Continue opens
  once the keys are accepted. No `fields` or `confirm`.

The guide is not part of the catalog fingerprint: rewording it does not mark
installed connectors as out of date. Progress is kept in the browser, with
the id of a connector saved by a `saveAndCheck` step, so a user coming back
days later continues with the keys they entered.

### Adapter file errors

If an adapter file cannot be read, check that its path exists and that the
validator process has permission to read it. This is distinct from invalid JSON
syntax, which requires fixing the file contents.

---

## 1. Parameters (JSON Schema)

Standard JSON Schema that defines tool inputs visible to the AI:

```json
{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "user_id": { "type": "integer", "description": "The user's ID" },
    "include_details": { "type": "boolean", "description": "Include extra details" },
    "query": { "type": "string", "description": "Search query" }
  },
  "required": ["user_id"]
}
```

Supported types: `string`, `integer`, `number`, `boolean`, `array`, `object`

> **Tip:** Parameters matching environment variable names are automatically stripped from the tool schema, so the AI never sees them.

---

## 2. Endpoint Mapping

The bridge configuration that transforms MCP tool calls into API requests.

### REST Example

```json
{
  "method": "POST",
  "path": "/users/{user_id}/orders",
  "queryParams": {
    "page": "$page",
    "limit": "$limit"
  },
  "bodyMapping": {
    "productId": "$product_id",
    "quantity": "$qty"
  },
  "headers": {
    "X-Request-ID": "$request_id"
  }
}
```

### Mapping Patterns

| Pattern | Location | Description |
|---------|----------|-------------|
| `{param}` in path | URL path | Replaced in URL: `/users/{id}` becomes `/users/123` |
| `"$param"` in queryParams | Query string | Added as `?param=value` |
| `"$param"` in bodyMapping | JSON body | Included in request body |
| `"$param"` in headers | HTTP headers | Sent as request header |
| `"Bearer ${param}"` in headers | HTTP headers | Interpolated; the header is left out when any `${…}` is empty or unset |

The `$` prefix means "take the value from the tool input parameter with this name."
Connector variables are available the same way, so an optional key is written as
`"headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${MY_API_KEY}" }`: sent when the variable is set, omitted
when it is empty, rather than going out as `Authorization: Bearer ` with nothing after it.

The same rule drops a whole string when one of its `${…}` placeholders has no value. That matters
for APIs that take a query language in one field (Google Ads GAQL, SOQL, JQL): a missing optional
filter would drop the entire query. Give such parameters a JSON-Schema `default` that matches
everything, and the tool call fills it in before the string is built:

```json
"parameters": { "properties": {
  "campaign_name": { "type": "string", "default": "%" },
  "limit": { "type": "integer", "default": 200 }
} },
"endpointMapping": { "method": "POST", "path": "/customers/{customer_id}/googleAds:search",
  "bodyMapping": { "query": "SELECT campaign.name FROM campaign WHERE campaign.name LIKE '${campaign_name}' LIMIT ${limit}" } }
```

A `{param}` value is inserted verbatim, slashes included, so a file path can span several segments. When
the identifier is itself a URL (a Search Console property such as `https://www.example.com/`, a sitemap
URL), set `"encodePathParams": true` on the mapping and every substituted value is percent-encoded
(`https%3A%2F%2Fwww.example.com%2F`). The model then passes the value raw, as the API returned it.

### File uploads (multipart/form-data)

A `bodyMapping` entry can carry a `__file` marker instead of a plain `"$param"` string.
Only valid when `bodyEncoding` is `"form-data"`:

```json
{
  "bodyEncoding": "form-data",
  "bodyMapping": {
    "image": { "__file": "$image_url" }
  }
}
```

The tool input parameter (`image_url` here) is a **URL**, not file content — there is no way
for an MCP tool call to carry raw bytes. The connector fetches that URL server-side (through the
same SSRF guard as every other outbound request, capped by `MAX_FILE_UPLOAD_BYTES`, 10 MB by
default) and attaches the response as a real multipart part, with a filename and content-type
instead of a text field containing the URL. Declare the parameter with `"type": "string",
"format": "uri"` so the model knows to pass a link. `__file` in a `form-urlencoded` body is a
configuration error — that encoding cannot carry a file at all.

### JSON-encoded fields (`__json`)

Some APIs take a method's arguments as one field holding JSON text, e.g. a form body
`method=getOrders&parameters={"order_id":42}`. Wrap that field in a `__json` marker and it goes
out as the JSON text of its resolved value:

```json
{
  "bodyEncoding": "form-urlencoded",
  "bodyMapping": {
    "method": "getOrders",
    "parameters": { "__json": { "order_id": "$order_id", "status_id": "$status_id" } }
  }
}
```

Arguments the caller leaves out are dropped first, so the example sends `{"order_id":42}` when only
`order_id` is given, and `{}` when nothing is. `{ "__json": "$order" }` passes a whole object
argument through. The marker works in JSON bodies too, where the field becomes a string. Only
markers written in the tool's own mapping count; one inside a caller's argument is an ordinary object.

### XML bodies

APIs that take an XML request (TallyPrime, SOAP-like endpoints) get their body
from a `__raw` string, or from a `bodyTemplate`, with `${param}` placeholders.
Set `"bodyEncoding": "xml"` on the mapping and every substituted value is
XML-escaped (`&` `<` `>` `"` `'`), so a name such as `Sharma & Sons` cannot
break the document:

```json
{
  "method": "POST",
  "path": "/",
  "bodyEncoding": "xml",
  "bodyMapping": {
    "__raw": "<ENVELOPE><SVCURRENTCOMPANY>${company}</SVCURRENTCOMPANY></ENVELOPE>"
  }
}
```

- Connector variables (`{{VAR}}`) in the body are escaped the same way.
- An `&` that already starts an entity (`&amp;`, `&#38;`, `&lt;` ...) is left
  as it is, so a value escaped by hand is not escaped twice.
- A whole-value `"__raw": "$param"` is the caller's own document and goes out
  unchanged.
- With `bodyEncoding: "xml"` a `bodyTemplate` is sent as text; it is not
  parsed as JSON. A missing placeholder becomes empty.
- The body is labelled `application/xml; charset=utf-8` unless the connector
  or the tool sets its own `Content-Type`.

Without `bodyEncoding: "xml"`, `__raw` values are inserted as they are, as
before.

### Response headers and pagination (`exposeHeaders`)

By default a tool receives the response **body** and nothing else. Some APIs put
the one thing a model needs to continue in a header instead: GitHub, GitLab,
Sentry and Shopify paginate with `Link: <...?cursor=xyz>; rel="next"`, and most
APIs report rate limits in `X-RateLimit-*`. Without those, every list tool is
exactly one page long.

A REST tool can opt in per header name (case-insensitive):

```json
{
  "method": "GET",
  "path": "/organizations/{{SENTRY_ORG}}/issues/",
  "queryParams": { "cursor": "$cursor", "query": "$query" },
  "exposeHeaders": ["link", "x-ratelimit-remaining"]
}
```

The selected headers are added to the tool result next to the body, and a
`Link` header with `rel="next"` is parsed for you:

```json
{
  "...the body as before...": "",
  "_headers": { "link": "<https://sentry.io/api/0/...?cursor=1568:0:0>; rel=\"next\"", "x-ratelimit-remaining": "39" },
  "_pagination": { "nextUrl": "https://sentry.io/api/0/...?cursor=1568:0:0", "nextCursor": "1568:0:0", "cursorParam": "cursor" }
}
```

- `_pagination` is **absent on the last page**; tell the model so in the tool description ("call again with `cursor` = `_pagination.nextCursor` until it is missing").
- `nextCursor` is recognised for the usual parameter names (`cursor`, `page`, `offset`, `after`, `page_token`, `starting_after`, ...); otherwise only `nextUrl` is set.
- If the body is not a JSON object (an array, a string) it is wrapped as `data` so the extras have somewhere to live.
- A response transform (`responseMapping.transform`) runs on the body first; the extras are attached afterwards, so a `select` cannot drop them.
- The audit log keeps storing the bare body. Headers are cached together with it when `cacheTtl` is set.
- REST connectors only. Tools that did not set `exposeHeaders` behave exactly as before.

### Slow or large responses (`timeoutMs`, `maxResponseBytes`)

A REST call times out after 30 s, and the engine stops reading an upstream body
larger than `TOOL_MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES` (10 MB by default). Image generation needs
more of both: a 2K or 4K picture can take a minute, and its base64 inside the
JSON can pass 10 MB before [`images`](<https://github.com/HelpCode-ai/anythingmcp/blob/main/docs/tool-definition.md#images-in-the-response-images>) takes it
out of the result. A tool can set its own values on the endpoint mapping:

```json
{
  "method": "POST",
  "path": "/models/{model}:generateContent",
  "timeoutMs": 120000,
  "maxResponseBytes": 41943040
}
```

- `timeoutMs`: milliseconds, clamped to 1 000 – 180 000. Absent: 30 000.
- `maxResponseBytes`: bytes of the upstream body, at most 50 MB (52 428 800), or
  `TOOL_MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES` when that is set higher. A lower value than the
  global one is allowed. Absent: `TOOL_MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES`.
- `maxResponseBytes` only applies to the body the API sends. The result text the
  client receives is still held to `TOOL_MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES`, so raise it only
  where `responseMapping` takes the bulk out (base64 images).
- A call that times out with a raised `timeoutMs` is not retried, whatever its
  method; a POST, PATCH or DELETE is never retried after a timeout anyway.
- REST connectors only. Tools without these keys behave exactly as before, on
  Cloud and self-hosted alike.

### Download links in the response (`download`)

Some APIs answer with a short-lived link to the data instead of the data
(Amazon SP-API report documents: `{ "url": "https://…amazonaws.com/…",
"compressionAlgorithm": "GZIP" }`). An AI client cannot open that link. With a
`download` block the tool makes its API call as usual, then fetches the link on
the server and returns the parsed content:

```json
"endpointMapping": {
  "method": "GET",
  "path": "/reports/2021-06-30/documents/{reportDocumentId}",
  "download": {
    "urlField": "url",
    "compressionField": "compressionAlgorithm",
    "format": "auto",
    "allowedHosts": ["amazonaws.com"],
    "offset": "$offset",
    "limit": "$limit",
    "columns": "$columns",
    "filterColumn": "$filterColumn",
    "filterValue": "$filterValue"
  }
}
```

- `urlField` (required): dot path of the link in the API response.
- `allowedHosts` (required): hosts the link may point to; a domain also matches
  its subdomains. Only `https` links are fetched.
- `compressionField`: dot path of a marker whose value `GZIP` means gunzip. Gzip
  is also recognised by its first bytes.
- `format`: `auto` (default) picks JSON, tab- or comma-separated text from the
  content; or `tsv`, `csv`, `json`, `text`.
- `offset`, `limit`, `columns`, `filterColumn`, `filterValue`: references to tool
  parameters. Delimited files come back as one page of rows keyed by the header
  (`limit` default 50, at most 500), filtered by one column (several values
  comma-separated, case-insensitive) and cut to the listed columns, with
  `columns`, `totalRows`, `matchedRows` and `nextOffset`. JSON comes back whole
  under `data`; other text as the first 20 000 characters.
- The link is fetched without the connector's credentials, with the same SSRF
  checks as every outbound call (each redirect included), at most 25 MB
  compressed and 32 MB decompressed.
- REST connectors only, on Cloud and self-hosted alike. Tools without the block
  behave exactly as before.

### By Connector Type

| Connector | method | path | queryParams | bodyMapping | headers |
|-----------|--------|------|-------------|-------------|---------|
| **REST** | HTTP method (`GET`, `POST`, etc.) | URL path with `{param}` | Query string params | JSON body fields | HTTP headers |
| **OData** | HTTP method, or a built-in `odata_list_services` / `odata_describe_service` / `odata_describe_entity` / `odata_query` / `odata_get` (see [OData](<https://github.com/HelpCode-ai/anythingmcp/blob/main/docs/connectors/odata.md>)) | Service path + entity set, with `{param}` | OData options (`$filter`, `$select`…) | JSON body fields | HTTP headers |
| **GraphQL** | `query` or `mutation` | The GraphQL query string | GraphQL variables (see [GraphQL variables](<https://github.com/HelpCode-ai/anythingmcp/blob/main/docs/tool-definition.md#graphql-variables>)) | — (ignored) | HTTP headers |
| **SOAP** | SOAP operation name | Port/binding path | — | SOAP parameters | HTTP headers |
| **Database** | `query` or `static` | SQL/MongoDB query with `$param` | — | — | — |
| **MCP** | Remote tool name | — | — | Passed through | — |
| **Email** | `static`, or a built-in `email_list_folders` / `email_search` / `email_get_message` / `email_get_attachment` / `email_set_flags` / `email_move` / `email_delete` / `email_save_draft` / `email_send` (see [Email](<https://github.com/HelpCode-ai/anythingmcp/blob/main/docs/connectors/email.md>)) | — | — | — (arguments are read directly) | — |

### Static tools

`"method": "static"` returns text stored on the tool, with no call to the upstream system: playbooks, example queries, domain guides. `staticResponse` is returned whatever the arguments. `staticResponses` holds several texts keyed by topic, chosen by the `topic` argument (or the argument named by `topicParam`); without a topic, or with an unknown one, the tool answers with `staticResponse` followed by the list of topics:

```json
{
  "name": "sap_guide",
  "parameters": { "type": "object", "properties": { "topic": { "type": "string", "enum": ["basics", "finance"] } } },
  "endpointMapping": {
    "method": "static",
    "path": "",
    "staticResponse": "How to read the SAP data model…",
    "staticResponses": { "basics": "Client, dates, currencies…", "finance": "The Universal Journal ACDOCA…" }
  }
}
```

### GraphQL Example

```json
{
  "method": "query",
  "path": "query GetUser($id: ID!) { user(id: $id) { id name email } }",
  "queryParams": {
    "id": "$user_id"
  }
}
```

For generic tools that take the GraphQL operation **as input**, set `path` to a `$paramName` reference and use `variablesFromParam` to forward the variables map verbatim:

```json
{
  "method": "query",
  "path": "$query",
  "variablesFromParam": "variables"
}
```

The GraphQL engine also supports `"method": "static"`, which returns `path` verbatim with no HTTP call — useful for tools that just need to expose a fixed value (e.g. the URL of the SDL schema).

#### GraphQL builtin tools (auto-injected)

Every adapter with `connector.type === "GRAPHQL"` is automatically extended with four generic tools:

- `<slug>_graphql_schema_url` — returns the URL of the SDL schema (default `${baseUrl}/schema`, override via `connector.schemaUrl`)
- `<slug>_graphql_query` — execute an arbitrary `query`
- `<slug>_graphql_mutation` — execute an arbitrary `mutation`
- `<slug>_graphql_subscription` — execute an arbitrary `subscription` (transport availability depends on the upstream API)

Adapter authors don't need to declare them. To install some of them switched off, list their suffixes in `connector.config.graphqlBuiltinsOff`, e.g. `["mutation", "subscription"]` when the token can reach destructive mutations the curated tools leave out. Admins can still switch them on per connector.

### GraphQL variables

The GraphQL engine builds the request's `variables` from exactly two places:

- `queryParams` — one **flat** entry per variable, keyed by the variable name as the operation declares it, whose value is `"$toolParam"` or a literal;
- `variablesFromParam` — the whole map, taken from one tool parameter (generic tools only).

Nothing else is read. `bodyMapping` in particular is ignored, so `"bodyMapping": { "variables": { … } }` sends `"variables": {}` on every call, and a `$param` nested inside a `queryParams` object is sent as the literal text `"$param"`. Where an API takes an input object, declare one variable per field and build the object inside the operation:

```json
{
  "method": "mutation",
  "path": "mutation CreateCustomer($businessId: ID!, $name: String!, $email: String) { customerCreate(input: { businessId: $businessId, name: $name, email: $email }) { didSucceed } }",
  "queryParams": { "businessId": "$business_id", "name": "$name", "email": "$email" }
}
```

`node scripts/validate-adapters.mjs` enforces this for `GRAPHQL` adapters (rule `graphql-variables`): no `bodyMapping`, no nested `$param` in `queryParams`, every `queryParams` key declared by the operation, every non-null variable without a default supplied, and every `"$name"` a tool parameter or an env var. A `REST` connector that POSTs to a `/graphql` path builds its body with `bodyMapping` as usual and is not affected.

### SOAP Example

```json
{
  "method": "GetCustomerDetails",
  "path": "CustomerServiceSoap12/BasicHttpBinding",
  "bodyMapping": {
    "customerId": "$customer_id",
    "includeHistory": "$include_history"
  }
}
```

### Database Example (SQL)

`${name}` placeholders are compiled to the driver's bound parameters
(`$1`, `?`, `:1`), so values are never spliced into the statement.

```json
{
  "method": "query",
  "path": "SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = ${customer_id} AND status = ${status} ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT ${limit}"
}
```

### Database Example (MongoDB)

The path is a JSON find spec — `collection` plus optional `filter`,
`projection`, `sort` and `limit`. `mongo_schema` takes no path at all and
lists the collections with a sampled field list.

```json
{
  "method": "query",
  "path": "{\"collection\": \"orders\", \"filter\": {\"customerId\": \"${customer_id}\"}, \"sort\": {\"createdAt\": -1}, \"limit\": ${limit}}"
}
```

### MCP Bridge Example

```json
{
  "method": "remote_tool_name",
  "bodyMapping": {
    "param1": "$param1",
    "param2": "$param2"
  }
}
```

`path` is optional here: omit it and the call goes to the connector's base URL
(or `<host>/mcp` if the base URL has no path). Set it only to send this one tool
somewhere else — see [MCP Bridge](<https://github.com/HelpCode-ai/anythingmcp/blob/main/docs/connectors/mcp-bridge.md>).

---

## 3. Response Mapping (Optional)

Shapes the API response **before it reaches the AI client**. Two reasons to use
it: keeping fields that should never travel out of the model's context, and not
paying for upstream noise in the context window.

The mapping is applied on the way out, so anything you drop never reaches the
agent or the model provider behind it. Your audit log still records the full
upstream response, so shaping the answer does not cost you the evidence of what
the API actually returned.

```json
{
  "transform": {
    "mode": "select",
    "exclude": ["customer.iban", "customer.taxId"],
    "select": { "order": "$.id", "total": "$.amounts.gross", "status": "$.state" }
  },
  "cacheTtl": 3600
}
```

| Field | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| `mode` | `select` (declarative template), `jmespath` (evaluate `expression`), or `off` to keep the config without applying it |
| `exclude` | Paths to drop, applied before everything else. The lever for PII and secrets |
| `include` | Keep only these paths, preserving the original document shape |
| `select` | Output template: keys are output names, leaves are paths (`$.a.b[*].c`) or literals |
| `expression` | JMESPath expression, for reshaping a template cannot express |
| `fallbackToRaw` | On error, return the raw response instead of failing. Default `true` |
| `maxBytes` | Hard cap on the serialized output. `0` or absent means no cap. It shapes a response that was read; the instance-wide `TOOL_MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES` (10 MB by default) decides whether the upstream body is read at all, and caps the text sent to the client (compact JSON first, then the `TOOL_RESPONSE_TOO_LARGE` error) |
| `cacheTtl` | Seconds to cache the **raw** upstream response; shaping happens on read |
| `images` | Paths to base64 images in the response, returned to the client as MCP image content (see below) |
| `binary` | How a file the API returns as raw bytes is handed over: `{ "as": "auto" \| "base64", "maxBytes": n }` (see below) |

### Images in the response (`images`)

Image generation APIs return the picture as base64 inside the JSON (OpenAI's
`data[].b64_json`, Gemini's `candidates[].content.parts[].inlineData.data`).
As text that is megabytes the model cannot look at. `images` lists where those
strings are, and each one is returned as an MCP `image` content block after the
text of the result:

```json
{ "images": { "paths": ["data[*].b64_json"], "maxImages": 4, "maxBytes": 4194304 } }
```

- Paths use keys, `[n]` and `[*]`. A single path or a list of paths is accepted
  as a shorthand for `{ "paths": [...] }`.
- The text keeps a placeholder where each image was (`[image 1: image/png,
  1.2 MB, attached to this result as an image]`), so a client that does not
  show images still learns what was returned. A `transform` runs after the
  images are taken out and sees the placeholders.
- Only PNG, JPEG, GIF and WebP leave as images, recognised by their first
  bytes rather than by what the API says. Anything else at those paths is
  replaced by a placeholder, never passed on as text.
- `maxImages` (default 4, at most 10) and `maxBytes` per image (decoded,
  default 4 MiB, at most 8 MiB) are capped, and all images of one result
  together at 12 MiB. An image over a limit is replaced by a placeholder that
  says why.
- Tools without `images` are not affected.

### Files in the response (`binary`)

A REST tool that downloads a file gets its bytes, not text: an image, a PDF,
an archive. Before October 2026 every body was decoded as UTF-8, which
corrupted a file (a Telegram download from
`https://api.telegram.org/file/bot<token>/<file_path>`, an invoice PDF).

The engine decides from the response itself:

- A text content type (`text/*`, JSON, XML, `image/svg+xml`, form data, CSV,
  YAML) is decoded and parsed as before: JSON when it parses, the string
  otherwise.
- `application/octet-stream`, or no content type at all, is treated as text
  when the bytes are valid UTF-8 without control characters, and as a file
  otherwise.
- Anything else is a file.

A file is handed to the client after the text of the result:

- A PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP becomes MCP `image` content. The type is
  recognised from the first bytes, so an image sent as
  `application/octet-stream` still counts.
- Any other file becomes an embedded `resource` with a `blob`, its content
  type and its file name (from `Content-Disposition`).
- The text describes the file (`contentType`, `bytes`, `size`, `filename`)
  and never contains the bytes.

A response mapping (`transform`, `images`, `decode`) does not apply to a
file. Neither the call log nor the dashboard's tool test stores the bytes.

```json
{ "binary": { "as": "base64", "maxBytes": 2097152 } }
```

- `maxBytes` per file: 4 MiB by default, at most 10 MiB. A larger file is
  described and not attached. A response body over `TOOL_MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES`
  (10 MB by default) is not read at all: the call fails with code
  `TOOL_RESPONSE_TOO_LARGE`.
- `as: "base64"` puts the base64 into the text (`file.base64`) instead of
  attaching it, for a workflow that hands the file on to another tool.
- Both keys are optional. A tool without `binary` gets the defaults.

### `select` leaf syntax

| Leaf | Result |
|------|--------|
| `"$.a.b"` / `"a.b"` | Path lookup. The key is omitted when the path is not found |
| `"= [redacted]"` | The static string `[redacted]`. Leading `=` marks a literal, so a constant is not mistaken for a path |
| `42`, `true`, `null` | Passed through as-is |
| `{ "$from": "$.rows[*]", "$select": { … } }` | Iterate an array and reshape every element |
| `{ … }` / `[ … ]` | Nested template / array of the above |

Paths accept `$.a.b`, `a[0].b`, `a[*].b` and `a['weird.key']`. A leading `$.` is
optional. Depth, path count and output size are bounded, so a pathological
response or template cannot pin a worker.

**Masking rather than dropping.** `exclude` removes a field outright, which
changes the shape of the response. When an agent is better served by a stable
shape, replace the value instead:

```json
{ "transform": { "mode": "select", "select": {
  "order": "$.id",
  "customer": "$.customer.name",
  "iban": "= [redacted]"
} } }
```

**In the UI:** the tool editor has a Response Mapping panel with the same three
modes and a **live preview** that runs the mapping against a real response and
reports the before/after size. A tool with a broken mapping is flagged in the
tool list rather than failing silently.

> A tool without a mapping behaves exactly as before — same object, byte for
> byte. The no-op path is the one that must never regress.

---

## 4. Tool Annotations (Optional)

Annotations are the [MCP spec's](<https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification>) advisory hints that let an
agent reason about a tool *before* calling it — above all whether it can change anything. An agent that
knows a tool is read-only will probe it freely instead of asking for confirmation.

| Hint | Spec default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `title` | — | Human-readable title for display |
| `readOnlyHint` | `false` | The tool does not modify its environment |
| `destructiveHint` | `true` | The write removes/overwrites rather than only adding. Meaningful only when `readOnlyHint` is false |
| `idempotentHint` | `false` | Repeating the call with the same arguments changes nothing further. Meaningful only when `readOnlyHint` is false |
| `openWorldHint` | `true` | Interacts with an external system of unbounded scope |

> Annotations are hints, not access control. The spec states clients must never make trust decisions based
> on them. Real enforcement stays in roles and per-tool access.

### Derived automatically

You normally do not set these. AnythingMCP derives them from what the connector already declares:

| Connector | Signal | Result |
|---|---|---|
| REST | `GET` / `HEAD` / `OPTIONS` | read-only |
| REST | `POST` | write, additive, non-idempotent |
| REST | `PUT` / `DELETE` | write, destructive, idempotent |
| REST | `PATCH` | write, destructive, non-idempotent |
| GraphQL | `query` / `mutation` | read-only / write |
| Database | connector `readOnly` flag, or `SELECT` vs `INSERT`/`UPDATE`/`DELETE` in the statement | read-only / write; always `openWorldHint: false` |
| Any | `static` method (fixed text, no call) | read-only |
| OData / REST | `odata_*` built-in methods | read-only |
| SOAP | operation name only | never asserts read-only; flags a clearly-named destructive op |
| MCP bridge | the upstream server's own annotations | passed through verbatim |

An unambiguous tool name (`delete_…`, `create_…`) refines `destructiveHint`, but **name heuristics never
assert `readOnlyHint`**: wrongly claiming read-only would invite an agent to call a mutating tool freely,
whereas omitting the hint only makes it more careful.

Once the read/write verdict is known, all three of `readOnlyHint`, `destructiveHint` and `idempotentHint`
are emitted explicitly. A read-only tool gets `destructiveHint: false` and `idempotentHint: true`; a write
with nothing better known gets the spec defaults. Some directory reviewers (OpenAI's plugin portal, for
one) reject a tool whose `destructiveHint` is missing, even a read-only one, so nothing is left implicit.

### Overriding

The one case the derivation cannot solve is a **read-only endpoint exposed over `POST`** — very common for
search APIs, and indistinguishable from a write at the protocol level. Fix it per tool, in the UI via the
tool's **Hints** button, or over the API:

```bash
# Mark a POST-based search as read-only
curl -X PATCH .../api/connectors/<connectorId>/tools/<toolId>/annotations \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"annotations": {"readOnlyHint": true}}'

# Inspect derived vs override vs effective
curl .../api/connectors/<connectorId>/tools/<toolId>/annotations -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'

# Drop the override, go back to derived
curl -X PATCH .../api/connectors/<connectorId>/tools/<toolId>/annotations \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"annotations": null}'
```

An override survives a re-import. Annotations coming from an *upstream MCP server* are refreshed on
re-import, since that server is authoritative about its own tools.

A catalog adapter that knows better can ship the override itself, as an `annotations` object on the tool
(`"annotations": {"readOnlyHint": true}`). It seeds the same per-tool override at install, so the operator
can still change it, and a catalog re-sync never overwrites it on a tool that already exists.

---

## 5. Caller-Context Variables (`{{amcp.*}}`)

Connectors often front a **service**-based API while users authenticate to AnythingMCP individually (OAuth,
per-user MCP API keys). The target system then only ever sees the service identity and cannot record who
actually asked. These reserved variables forward the calling identity so it can — in headers, query
parameters, the body, or the path:

```json
{
  "method": "POST",
  "path": "/tickets",
  "headers": {
    "X-Requested-By": "{{amcp.user_email}}"
  },
  "bodyMapping": {
    "subject": "$subject",
    "requestedBy": "{{amcp.user_email}}"
  }
}
```

| Variable | Value |
|---|---|
| `{{amcp.user_email}}` | E-mail of the calling user |
| `{{amcp.user_id}}` | Internal user id |
| `{{amcp.org_id}}` | Workspace (organization) id |
| `{{amcp.server_id}}` | Id of the MCP server that exposed the tool |
| `{{amcp.server_name}}` | Name of that MCP server |
| `{{amcp.auth_method}}` | `jwt`, `mcp_api_key`, `static_api_key`, `static_bearer` or `none` |
| `{{amcp.api_key_name}}` | Name of the MCP API key used, when applicable |

Behaviour worth knowing:

- **Opt-in.** Nothing is forwarded unless you write the variable somewhere. Identity is personal data, so it
  is never attached automatically.
- **Not always available.** Identity exists for OAuth and per-user MCP API keys. With an instance-wide static
  API key or bearer token, and in anonymous mode, there is no user — the variable resolves to an **empty
  string** rather than leaking a literal `{{amcp.…}}` to the target.
- **Non-spoofable.** The values are resolved server-side from the authenticated request and merged *after*
  connector env vars, so neither a workspace variable nor a tool argument can shadow them. Users cannot
  change their own e-mail address either (`PUT /api/users/me` refuses a new one, on Cloud and self-hosted),
  so `{{amcp.user_email}}` is the address the account was created with, or the one your identity provider
  sets through SCIM.
- **Typos are rejected** when you save the tool, since at runtime an unknown reserved variable would silently
  resolve to empty.
- These variables apply to `baseUrl`, connector headers and the whole endpoint mapping — `path`,
  `queryParams`, `bodyMapping` **and `bodyTemplate`**. In a `bodyTemplate` the substituted value is escaped
  for its JSON string context, so a quote or backslash cannot break the document. They are **not**
  substituted inside `authConfig`.
- The **Test** button in the connector UI does not run through an authenticated MCP session, so `{{amcp.*}}`
  resolves to empty there; the test result says so. Call the tool from a connected MCP client to see the
  real value.

---

## Full Tool Example

```json
{
  "name": "search_products",
  "description": "Search products by keyword and category",
  "parameters": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "query": { "type": "string", "description": "Search keyword" },
      "category": { "type": "string", "description": "Product category" },
      "limit": { "type": "integer", "description": "Max results (default 10)" }
    },
    "required": ["query"]
  },
  "endpointMapping": {
    "method": "GET",
    "path": "/api/products/search",
    "queryParams": {
      "q": "$query",
      "cat": "$category",
      "limit": "$limit"
    }
  },
  "responseMapping": {
    "transform": {
      "select": {
        "total": "$.meta.totalCount",
        "products": {
          "$from": "$.data[*]",
          "$select": {
            "id": "id",
            "name": "attributes.name",
            "price": "attributes.price.amount",
            "category": "relationships.category.name"
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}
```

`responseMapping.transform` shapes the response before it reaches the AI client —
fewer tokens, and only the fields this tool needs leave the workspace. It is
optional: without it the raw upstream response is returned unchanged. See
[REST connector → Response Mapping](<https://github.com/HelpCode-ai/anythingmcp/blob/main/docs/connectors/rest.md#response-mapping>) for the
full syntax (`select`, `include`, `exclude`, JMESPath, `maxBytes`) — it applies
to every connector type, not just REST.

---

## Authentication: `LOGIN_TOKEN`

In addition to the standard `NONE` / `API_KEY` / `BEARER_TOKEN` / `BASIC_AUTH` / `OAUTH2` / `QUERY_AUTH` / `WS_SECURITY` / `CERTIFICATE` / `CONNECTION_STRING` schemes, the connector spec supports `LOGIN_TOKEN` for APIs that issue a long-lived bearer **in exchange for a credentials POST** — optionally requiring the password to be **bcrypt-hashed with a salt fetched from the remote service** (Sorare-style). APIs that log in with a JWT the client signs with its own private key instead of a password (noon's Partner API) use `signedJwt`.

The engine handles salt fetch → bcrypt → login → token cache → proactive refresh → re-login-on-401 automatically. Adapter authors declare the full flow as JSON:

```json
{
  "authType": "LOGIN_TOKEN",
  "authConfig": {
    "loginUrl": "https://api.example.com/graphql",
    "loginMethod": "POST",
    "loginBody": {
      "query": "mutation Login($email: String!, $password: String!) { signIn(input: {email: $email, password: $password}) { jwtToken { token expiredAt } } }",
      "variables": { "email": "${username}", "password": "${passwordHashed}" }
    },
    "username": "{{SERVICE_EMAIL}}",
    "password": "{{SERVICE_PASSWORD}}",
    "aud": "{{SERVICE_AUD}}",
    "passwordHashing": {
      "scheme": "bcrypt",
      "saltSource": {
        "type": "fetch",
        "method": "GET",
        "url": "https://api.example.com/api/v1/users/${username}",
        "responsePath": "salt"
      },
      "outputParam": "passwordHashed"
    },
    "tokenJsonPath": "data.signIn.jwtToken.token",
    "expiryJsonPath": "data.signIn.jwtToken.expiredAt",
    "expiryFormat": "iso8601",
    "tokenTTLSeconds": 2592000,
    "refreshOn401": true,
    "proactiveRefreshSeconds": 86400,
    "headerName": "Authorization",
    "headerTemplate": "Bearer ${token}",
    "extraHeaders": { "JWT-AUD": "${aud}" }
  }
}
```

A login that takes HTTP Basic credentials (Wazuh's `POST /security/user/authenticate`) sets `"loginBasicAuth": true`: the engine sends `Authorization: Basic base64(username:password)` on the login request only (the API calls keep using `headerTemplate`), the password is never offered to the body templates (`${password}` renders empty), and no body is sent without a `loginBody`. An `Authorization` in `loginHeaders` is refused rather than overridden, as are `signedJwt`, bcrypt `passwordHashing` and a username containing `:`; `scripts/validate-adapters.mjs` reports the same mistakes (rule `login-basic-auth`).

When the login answer is not documented, `tokenJsonPath` may be a list of paths tried in order (the first non-empty string wins), e.g. `["AuthenticationResult.IdToken", "idToken", "token", "."]`.

See [`docs/connectors/login-token-auth.md`](<https://github.com/HelpCode-ai/anythingmcp/blob/main/docs/connectors/login-token-auth.md>) for the full field-by-field reference, salt-source types (`fetch` vs `static`), expiry formats (`iso8601` / `unix` / `ttl_seconds`), and re-login policies.

## docs/integrations/chatgpt.md

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HelpCode-ai/anythingmcp/main/docs/integrations/chatgpt.md

# Connect AnythingMCP to ChatGPT

> Setup guide for using AnythingMCP tools with ChatGPT.

[Back to README](<https://github.com/HelpCode-ai/anythingmcp/blob/main/README.md>)

---

## Overview

ChatGPT on the web can add a custom remote MCP server as a plugin, so you can use your AnythingMCP tools directly in ChatGPT conversations. No developer mode is needed. On Business, Enterprise and Edu workspaces the **Create plugins with MCPs** permission controls who can add one.

---

## Prerequisites

- ChatGPT on the web. On a **Business** workspace only admins and owners can add custom MCP servers; on **Enterprise** and **Edu** an admin can grant the **Create plugins with MCPs** permission under **Workspace settings → Permissions & roles**
- AnythingMCP deployed and accessible via a **public HTTPS URL** (ChatGPT connects from the cloud)
- MCP tools configured in your AnythingMCP instance

> **Important:** ChatGPT connects to MCP servers from the internet. Your AnythingMCP instance must be accessible via a public URL with HTTPS. A `localhost` URL will not work.

---

## Step 1: Deploy AnythingMCP Publicly

If you haven't already, deploy AnythingMCP with a public HTTPS URL. See the [Deployment Guide](<https://github.com/HelpCode-ai/anythingmcp/blob/main/docs/deployment.md>) for instructions on setting up a reverse proxy with TLS.

Your MCP endpoint will be:
```
https://mcp.yourdomain.com/mcp
```

---

## Step 2: Configure MCP Auth

ChatGPT's custom MCP server dialog offers **OAuth**, **No authentication**, or **OAuth or no authentication**. It has no field for a bearer token or API key, so use OAuth. Set the auth mode in your `.env` (`oauth2` is the default; `both` also keeps legacy tokens and API keys working for other clients) and set `SERVER_URL` to your public HTTPS URL, which OAuth uses for its metadata and redirects:

```env
MCP_AUTH_MODE=oauth2    # or 'both' for OAuth2 + legacy tokens / API keys
SERVER_URL=https://mcp.yourdomain.com
```

---

## Step 3: Add MCP Server in ChatGPT

1. Open **Plugins** in ChatGPT on the web: [chatgpt.com/plugins](<https://chatgpt.com/plugins>)
2. Click **Add** (top right), then **Add custom MCP server**
3. Enter a name (e.g. AnythingMCP) and an optional description
4. Under **Connection**, enter the **Server URL**: `https://mcp.yourdomain.com/mcp` (on AnythingMCP Cloud, the endpoint URL shown on your server's page)
5. Set **Authentication** to **OAuth**
6. Review the risk warning and select **I understand and want to continue**
7. Select **Create as a plugin** and sign in to AnythingMCP when asked

The plugin appears under your personal plugins ([chatgpt.com/plugins?view=personal](<https://chatgpt.com/plugins?view=personal>)). Install it there, and ChatGPT discovers the tools from your AnythingMCP instance.

---

## Step 4: Use Tools in Conversations

Once installed, type **@** in a chat, pick the plugin, and ask ChatGPT to use your MCP tools naturally:

- *"Use the CRM to look up customer John Smith"*
- *"Query the database for orders from last week"*
- *"Search our product catalog for wireless headphones"*

ChatGPT will call the appropriate MCP tool and show you the results.

---

## The fixed plugin endpoint: `/mcp/chatgpt-app`

`https://<your-host>/mcp/chatgpt-app` serves one fixed set of tools, the same for every user. It is the endpoint of the [AnythingMCP plugin in the ChatGPT Plugin Directory](<https://chatgpt.com/plugins/plugin_asdk_app_6ade03541ce08191b35bbad1dc5b4121>) (on AnythingMCP Cloud), whose guidelines require every operation to be its own tool. It does not run your connectors' own tools; use `/mcp/<server-id>` (or `/mcp`) for that.

| Tool | What it does |
|------|--------------|
| `anythingmcp_list_connectors` | Connectors the connection reaches, their type and setup state |
| `anythingmcp_list_databases` | Databases that can be queried, with their engine |
| `anythingmcp_get_database_schema` | Tables and columns of one database |
| `anythingmcp_get_query_examples` | Example queries in the database's dialect |
| `anythingmcp_query_database` | One read-only query (SQL `SELECT`, or a MongoDB find) |
| `anythingmcp_get_connector_activity` | Calls and failures per connector, counts only |
| `anythingmcp_get_workspace_guide` | The workspace's notes on its connectors |
| `anythingmcp_get_configuration_url` | Link to the dashboard |

Only database connectors set to **read-only** are queried; a connector with write access is listed as not queryable. API and application connectors (Odoo, Shopify and the like) are listed but not run here. `anythingmcp_list_connectors` then returns `otherConnectorsHint`, which tells the user to connect them to ChatGPT through the MCP server's own URL, following the ChatGPT steps on the server's page in the dashboard. The endpoint never returns server URLs itself. Sign-in, the server or workspace picker, MCP roles and the audit log work as on `/mcp`. The endpoint behaves the same on Cloud and on a self-hosted instance, and needs a signed-in user (OAuth or a per-user MCP API key), not the static `MCP_API_KEY` / `MCP_BEARER_TOKEN`.

---

## The File Search plugin endpoint: `/mcp/file-search`

`https://<your-host>/mcp/file-search` serves the File Search plugin ("SFTP & NAS Search by Helpcode" in the ChatGPT Plugin Directory). Like `/mcp/chatgpt-app`, it has one fixed set of tools, the same for every user, and each tool is one operation. It only reaches the workspace's File Search folders; catalog connectors, databases and the File Share connector are not served here.

| Tool | What it does |
|------|--------------|
| `list_file_sources` | The connected folders: protocol, content summary, indexed files, last sync, the admin's notes |
| `search_documents` | Full-text search over the documents, with the best page and a snippet; every folder when no `source` is given |
| `find_files` | Files by name or glob pattern |
| `list_folder` | One folder's subfolders and files |
| `read_document` | The text of one file, whole or by pages |
| `find_exact_text` | Exact codes, numbers and phrases with their lines (whole rows in spreadsheets) |
| `view_document_page` | One PDF page or an image as a picture |
| `get_file_link` | The original file as a 24-hour link for members of the workspace |

Every tool is read-only except `get_file_link`, which stores a members-only link. With more than one folder connected, the tools that take a path need `source` (the id or name `list_file_sources` returns). Roles, folder rules per role and the audit log work as on `/mcp`. When no folder is connected, the tools answer with the link to the File Search wizard instead.

### Folder setup while connecting

When ChatGPT asks for `/mcp/file-search` (its OAuth `resource`), a workspace admin whose workspace has no File Search folder yet sees one more page after **Approve**: how to reach the folder (SFTP, FTPS, FTP, WebDAV, Nextcloud, ownCloud, Synology, QNAP, FRITZ!Box, Hetzner Storage Box, S3-compatible storage, and on a self-hosted instance a mounted network folder). Each choice opens the File Search wizard in the dashboard, signed in on the workspace the connection was granted, with that protocol preselected and the granted MCP servers ticked. When the folder is activated, the wizard returns to the authorization and the browser goes back to ChatGPT. **Skip** goes back at once. Passwords and keys are entered in the wizard, never in the chat.

Editors, viewers and workspaces that already have a folder go straight back to ChatGPT. The page and the endpoint behave the same on Cloud and on a self-hosted instance; on a self-hosted Community edition, File Search itself needs its trial or a licence, which the wizard explains. Other clients and endpoints keep their pages: the first-connector page after **Approve** (Cloud) is unchanged for them.

---

## Authentication Options

| Method | Configuration |
|--------|--------------|
| **OAuth2** (recommended) | `MCP_AUTH_MODE=oauth2` or `both`; choose **OAuth** in ChatGPT's custom MCP server dialog |
| **Bearer Token** | Not supported by ChatGPT's dialog (no token field); use it from the Responses API or other MCP clients |
| **API Key** | Not supported by ChatGPT's dialog; use a per-user MCP API key from the Responses API (below) or other MCP clients |

### OpenAI Responses API

An agent built on the Responses API can reach an MCP server with a per-user MCP API key (`mcp_…`, generated on the server's page). Send it as `authorization`, which arrives as `Authorization: Bearer mcp_…`, or as an `X-API-Key` header:

```json
"tools": [
  {
    "type": "mcp",
    "server_label": "anythingmcp",
    "server_url": "https://cloud.anythingmcp.com/mcp/<server-id>",
    "authorization": "mcp_your_key",
    "require_approval": "never"
  }
]
```

---

## Troubleshooting

| Issue | Solution |
|-------|----------|
| "Cannot connect to server" | Ensure your AnythingMCP URL is publicly accessible via HTTPS |
| "Authentication failed" | Check that `MCP_AUTH_MODE` is `oauth2` or `both` and that `SERVER_URL` is your public HTTPS URL |
| "No tools found" | Check that connectors and tools are configured in AnythingMCP |
| Timeout errors | Check that your reverse proxy doesn't have aggressive timeout settings; MCP uses long-lived connections |

---

## Security Considerations

When exposing AnythingMCP to the internet for ChatGPT:

1. **Always use HTTPS** — Never expose MCP over plain HTTP
2. **Use strong tokens** — Generate long, random Bearer Tokens
3. **Enable rate limiting** — Set `MCP_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MINUTE` in `.env`
4. **Use roles** — Create a restricted MCP role for ChatGPT with only the tools it needs
5. **Monitor audit logs** — Review tool invocations in the AnythingMCP audit log

## docs/integrations/claude.md
